FINAL REPORT OF SELECT COMMITTEE PRESENTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to present the second and final report of the select committee on radio broadcasting. This report is unanimous, and copies are being printed in English and in French.
The select committee appointed on radio broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies of the corporation with special reference to revenues, expenditures and development, begs leave to present the following as its second and final report:
Your committee held seven meetings and had as principal witnesses the chairman and vice chairman of the board of governors and the general manager. During seven sittings, an exhaustive examination was conducted. All information required by the committee to carry out its terms of reference was supplied, confidential information not susceptible of publication in the public interest being made available privately. The committee was impressed by the ability and frankness of the principal witnesses.
The bulk of the evidence concerned the program, technical and financial policies of the corporation. Your committee is of the opinion that these policies are well designed to carry out the purpose for which the corporation was created. Your committee is also of the opinion that the policies of the corporation are being executed in a businesslike fashion.
With respect to programs, the corporation's policy is to utilize Canadian talent in the development of Canadian, programs of distinction and quality, and to make available to Canadians the best programs from the United States, Great Britain and elsewhere. With the resources at its disposal, your committee believes, the corporation can give Canada satisfactory broadcasting service, while at the same time enabling Canada to create programs worthy of exchange.
With respect to the corporation's plan of national coverage, involving the ownership of high power stations and the extension of CBC coverage to reach all parts of Canada, your committee wishes to indicate its approval. It is considered that the development of this plan is of great importance in the national interest. Your committee is of the opinion that while private stations will continue to serve a useful local purpose, the corporation urgently requires its own comprehensive facilities for distribution. At the present time, large areas of Canada, particularly in the maritimes, the prairies and British Columbia, receive somewhat scant and spasmodic service of CBC programs.
Your committee is satisfied that the financial policies of the corporation are sound and that the administration is being conducted in a prudent and efficient manner.
Your committee considered carefully the present and future revenue requirements of
the corporation. It is of the opinion that present sources of revenue should be sufficient to maintain and develop the projected plan of national coverage.
With respect to revenue for capital purposes, your committee is of the opinion that consideration should be given to the provision by loan or grant, of sufficient capital funds to enable the corporation to complete its plan of national coverage at the earliest possible moment.
Your committee is of the opinion that the present scale of licence fees of $50, for privately owned broadcasting stations of hundred watts or under is adequate, but believes licence fees should be increased on higher powered stations servicing densely populated areas.
Your committee recommends that the incidence of the application of the licence fee be carefully reviewed by the Department of Transport in the light of this year's experience, with a view of effecting a reduction of the licence fees.
Your committee was impressed with the importance of the establishment, at an early date, of a high power short-wave broadcasting station. Such a station, your committee believes, would be a great utility in interpreting and advertising Canada abroad and in facilitating an exchange of programs between Canada and other broadcasting systems. Canada, your committee was informed, is the only major trading nation without such facilities. It is submitted this should be financed as a national project, operated and controlled by the corporation.
Your committee believes that the constitution of the corporation, ensuring a proper division between policy and management and a degree of flexibility and independence essential to the medium of broadcasting, together with ultimate parliamentary control, is well suited to the purpose for which it was created. Public service broadcasting in Canada must necessarily continue to be free from partisan control, and your committee is gratified to report that the activities of the CBC have been free from any nature of partisanship whatsoever. Your committee also wished to pay its tribute to the governors of the corporation for their vision, public spirit and efficient conduct of the trust imposed upon them by parliament.
In conclusion, your committee wishes to express its belief that the broadcasting Bystem emerging in Canada is, and can increasingly be, an important factor in creating a sense of national unity and approves the general policy of concentrating on a national system-of high power stations.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Government of the Northwest Territories: general administration, operation, maintenance and improvement of services, including Wood Buffalo park, $245,320.

Would the minister explain the increase of $30,714.50 in this item?
Supply-Northwest Territories

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: The increase is due in part to the restoration of the salary deduction that was in effect for several years prior to last year, and to the annual statutory salary increases. There is also an increased amount for supplies and materials. In previous years practically all the government drug supplies required in the Northwest Territories were provided through the Indian Affairs branch, but under a rearrangement the Northwest Territories vote is charged with the amount this year. There is also an increased expenditure for provisions for destitute people in the Northwest Territories. Hon. members are familiar with the fur cycles in the Northwest Territories; these cycles come and go, and last year and this the cycle has been at a very low point; consequently the revenue derived by individuals from trapping has been reduced and more cases have required assistance from the administration. These are the main increases. There is also a small increase for hospitalization and an increase to restore fire fighting and other equipment at Fort Smith and Wood Buffalo park. Fort Smith is the administrative headquarters of the Mackenzie district.

There has been a good deal of talk and speculation, mostly in the newspapers, concerning the desire of British Columbia to annex certain portions of northern territory. Would the minister be kind enough to make a statement concerning any negotiations which have been carried on up to the present time, and what the probable outcome will be?

No negotiations have taken place on the mdtter to which my hon. friend alludes. Any discussions with British Columbia regarding the Yukon, which I understand the hon. member includes in his question, were brought down in a return to the house several months ago.

I see on page 112, itemized, a reduction in the number of head clerks from six to five at $3,000, $15,000; last year there were six, the amount being $16,500, a difference of $1,500. Will the minister kindly explain why the reduction is only $1,500? Were the six clerks in receipt of $3,000 each?
I am advised the explanation is that there is one clerk less this year.
Yes, I see that. It is shown in the estimates. But the difference is only $1,500.
I am advised that the clerk who has retired was paid $1,500 retiring leave which was coming to him when he retired. That is the explanation of the difference.
He had worked only part of the year?
Yes.
Where is Wood Buffalo park located?

Wood Buffalo park is
located partly in northern Alberta and partly in the Northwest Territories on the west side of the Athabaska river. It is a very large park, set aside many years ago. I am advised that it comprises 17,300 square miles. It was set aside for the purpose of providing a sanctuary for the wood buffalo. In more recent years some buffalo from the prairies have been moved to that park. It is really a game sanctuary, located in the northern part of Alberta and, to the extent of roughly one-third, in the Northwest Territories.

I mentioned a moment ago the desire of British Columbia to acquire more northern territory. That brings to mind an agitation which has been going on in parts of northern Alberta and northern British Columbia to form a new province in certain areas of those two provinces and to include in that new province certain parts of the Northwest Territories. I understand that petitions have been forwarded to the government and resolutions have been passed by various boards of trade advocating such a project. Would the minister tell us how far negotiations have gone and exactly how much there is to this agitation to form a new province by taking parts of northern Alberta, northern British Columbia and a part of the Northwest Territories? Has the matter been brought to the attention of the government? What action has been taken or what consideration is the government giving to a scheme of that kind?

Some petitions may have
gone to the Prime Minister's office. I do not recall that any came to the Department of Mines and Resources. As my hon. friend is, of course, aware, governments receive petitions and resolutions on all sorts of questions. I am aware only through the press that there has been some discussion in part of Alberta emphasizing the importance and desirability of creating a new province in that part of Canada. I would doubt if the circumstances are such as to warrant the greatly increased expenditure which such an undertaking would involve. All I can say is that I am certain that no negotiations have taken

Supply-Northwest Territories
place, although I should think it possible that some petitions or resolutions may have found their way to the office of some department of government.

I quite agree with the minister. My opinion is that we have a sufficient number of governments in Canada at the present time without creating any more:	We have enough taxing bodies, without adding devices to increase taxation. I do admit, however, that eventually, when development has progressed, the time may come when such a new division of territory will be required in Canada for the purposes of administration. But what I wanted to know from the minister was if there were any official negotiations, and I understand there are none-simply resolutions passed by various organizations demanding consideration of this problem. I agree with the minister that perhaps it is a matter for future consideration, but that at the present time the country has not developed sufficiently to justify consideration of the formation of a new province in that part of Canada.

Of course no such step
could be taken without legislation passed by this parliament. Whenever the time comes, if it is ever considered, it will have to be approved by parliament.

To put the matter
simply, there has been no official communication to that effect?
No.
Have the Eskimos begun yet to make use of the reindeer for food and clothing?

Yes. The reports that we get of the value of the reindeer quite support the view which was held when they were originally introduced to that part of the Northwest Territories. They are providing not only food but clothing. Consideration is being given to providing some of the more advanced Eskimos with a few head of reindeer with a view to domesticating the animals, as has happened in certain parts of Europe.
That was the idea originally, was it not?

I do not know that any concrete steps have yet been taken with regard to it. I understand that a small experiment is to be carried on in that direction this year. We are using the Eskimo wherever possible in herding the deer and looking after them, and in that way they are getting an acquaintanceship with them which, we hope, ultimately will
bring about a condition whereunder the Eskimos will have their own small herds and be dependent upon them. Not only can they get food and clothing by this means, but they probably can use them for transportation purposes, as they are used,-1 believe, in Lapland.
Are the reindeer being allowed to spread and breed and so populate the areas further north?
No, up to the present time they have all been kept in herd. That has to be done in order to protect them from the wolves, and to build up the herd.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a request which I have had from the young men's section of the Saskatoon board of trade to convey to the government their desire to retain a certain wild life exhibit in Prince Albert national park. I can place the case before the minister best by reading a letter I have received from the young men's section of the Saskatoon board of trade. It is addressed to myself and is as follows:
This exhibit is of great educational value and has proven an outstanding attraction for tourists and visitors to the park. We understand that Mr. Lund has received offers for his exhibit from United States interests and we believe that if no action to retain it is taken by the dominion government, it will be lost to Canada.
We feel that the dominion government should consider, as part of their policy to build museums throughout Canada, the possibility of constructing a building at the Prince Albert national park. Arrangements could be made with Mr. Lund for his exhibit and for himself to act as curator.
If this suggestion is carried out, the exhibit could be moved for the winter months to some larger centre in Saskatchewan for the benefit of winter visitors.
We strongly protest the action taken in asking Mr. Lund to remove his exhibit from the park and would greatly appreciate any assistance you may be able to give to have this fine exhibit retained in Canada and in Saskatchewan.
Can the minister give us any information with regard to this matter? Would they consider retaining that exhibit? It seems to be of great value from the tourist point of view.

The information in the
letter read by my hon. friend is not quite correct. Mr. Lund was not asked to remove the exhibit from the park. There were some negotiations with him with regard to the amount of money he should receive. The park officials thought the consideration he was asking was rather large, and, of course, if they had been unable to get together the exhibit would have -been removed. But arrangements have been made with Mr. Lund
Supply-Northwest Territories

to leave the exhibit in the park on the same terms as last year. The matter will be before me probably to-morrow, I am advised by my officials, and the arrangement will be carried through on that basis. The exhibit will remain in the park on the same basis as last year. There was no request to Mr. Lund to remove it from the park. I wish to make that very clear. There was 'a difference as to the amount of consideration that Mr. Lund thought he was entitled to, but that has been smoothed out in the way I have indicated.
My letter is dated May 3.
That probably explains it.
How many reindeer are in the Northwest Territories at the present time and what success has been achieved?
Will the hon. member be good enough to speak louder. There is a lot of talking going on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I would request
that there be less talking among hon: members. It is difficult to hear those who are speaking.
I was asking whether the minister could tell us the number of reindeer in the Northwest Territories at the present time.

A few months ago on the last report there were over 4,000. When they were brought into the region east of the Mackenzie delta there were 2,300 odd in the herd and that has increased now, according to the last report, to something over 4,000. The fawning season is on now.

Will the' minister please give me a breakdown of hospitalization, professional and other special services, grants to schools, assistance to industrial homes, $54,810? What does "professional and other special services" mean? Would that be medical and dental services?

These are the figures for Anglican missions: Hospitals, $13,245; day schools, $1,537-1 am giving only the dollars- residential schools, $9,137, a total of $23,919. For the Roman Catholic missions in the western Arctic: hospitals, $10,877; day schools, $1,750; residential schools, $10,360, or a totai of $22,987. There is just a little less than 81,000 difference in the amounts contributed under the various headings to the Church of England and the Roman Catholic missions.

There has been a great deal of development in the mining areas in the Northwest Territories in recent years,

and one of the great difficulties is the matter of hospitalization and medical assistance. I know that the government has been kind enough to give grants to various institutions that are carrying on that work; nevertheless the minister will undoubtedly agree with me that with the intensive development of the Northwest Territories additional hospitalization should be provided. Conditions in that part of Canada are not as elsewhere. The people are situated many hundreds of miles from any medical assistance whatever, and because of the value which northern mining has added to Canada's wealth I believe it is a matter which the department should seriously consider. Perhaps the minister would give an outline of present hospitalization plans which are fostered by the department in the Northwest Territories, at what places they are functioning, and the services they are rendering.

It is rather difficult to give any precise information at the moment. Mining development in the Northwest Territories is taking place of course, in the Great Bear Lake region where the Eldorado mines operate, and to the north of Great Slave lake in what is known as the Yellowknife country. The Eldorado mines have their own doctor at the mine and a small hospital with a few beds to look after those who may be suffering illness. That service, however, is confined almost entirely to their own employees. Outside that, the population in that particular area is small. When we come to the Slave lake country we find that development is only in its initial stages. The question is being studied by the officers and the council of the Northwest Territories administration, to make provision for what may be necessary in that regard. We aim to get the administration of these things on the most efficient basis possible. We are trying to plan a little ahead.

The policy of the
department in the past I believe has been to provide hospitalization for the Indians and the Eskimo in the northern part of the country by giving assistance to various missions. I commend the government for that. But I point out that times are changing, mining development is increasing, and now there are others in that country who perhaps have a claim on the department for additional assistance so far as hospitals and medical service are concerned. Some mining companies maintain their own doctors, who can render assistance in case of emergency; nevertheless in order to encourage development and take care of the people coming into the north country, including the increasing number

Supply-Northwest Territories
of prospectors who go in on their own, not for any company, facilities should be provided at certain points. I believe at present there is an opening for a doctor attached to the Northwest Territories administration. Does the department intend to fill that position? Instead of curtailing the services the department should realize the increasing needs and enlarge the services it has provided in the past.

We do not ourselves operate hospitals in the Northwest Territories; they are built either by the Anglican or by the Roman Catholic missions. In some cases we give a grant to assist in construction. For Indian patients and indigents who receive treatment in the hospitals we pay a per diem charge to the hospital. It is probable that a doctor will be appointed to the Fort Norman district before very long; the matter is now under consideration.
Does the construction and maintenance of highways in the national parks come under this item?
It comes under a later item.
Who makes the appointments in the national parks? Are they generally made through the recommendation of private members?

Practically all the appointments on the clerical and engineering staffs and that sort of thing are under the civil service commission certification. The expenditures under special supplementary estimates, and prior to that under the Public Works Construction Act of the late government, were exempt from the civil service commission's jurisdiction. Then there is another class, the labourers in the parks, who are not under the civil service commission. I can assure my hon. friend that we endeavour always to get the most capable men we can.
But who makes the appointments?
The appointments are made in the way they have been made for many years past. They are made by the superintendents and by the engineers.
Are they not made by the minister?
Sometimes on the approval of the minister, but I can assure my hon. friend that the practice in that respect is precisely what it was before.
Does the recommendation of a private member go very far?
Sometimes it is considered.

I think I have evidence that the private member's recommendation does not go very far. I have here a photograph of a letter signed by an hon. member of this house. It is dated April 8, 1937, addressed to Fred Duval, and reads as follows:
Dear Fred:
I have your letter of recent date re a position1 in the national park.
In reply, may I say that the only way you can get a position in the national park is to be recommended by the Prince Albert federal Liberal executive. I cannot see why anyone writes to any of the federal members of Saskatchewan about a position in Prince Albert national park when there has not been one position given in the park outside of the Prince Albert riding since it was started. Any person who tells you that anything else is different is just "passing the buck." That is all. Will you kindly go to the president of the federal Liberal executive of Prince Albert and take up the matter with him to see what can be done. That is the only way action can be got.
Who signed that?
It is signed " Cameron R. McIntosh."

I have no doubt that my hon. friend will place that in his archives and look at it occasionally with some satisfaction. I know nothing of the letter; this is the first time I have heard of it. But I repeat what I said a moment ago, which is as patent to the hon. member as to many other hon. members of the house, that the appointments in Prince Albert park are made in precisely the same way as they were made during the regime of the late government. In fact I would say there has been a substantial improvement as to the methods.
More Liberal appointments now.

No, no. This question may have its lighter aspects, but probably no one knows better than the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) the procedure which has usually obtained in these appointments. We do aim as far as possible to get those who are unemployed, and to the best of my knowledge there has not been discrimination in that respect.
This letter just sets out the procedure in getting appointments. Possibly some Liberal members from Saskatchewan can say how they are making out when they make recommendations.

To what extent has it been possible under that method of making appointments to maintain the preference for ex-service men?

Supply-Northwest Territories
As far as my knowledge goes that preference has been maintained.

The minister I am sure will forgive me if I again remind him of the importance of establishing a national park on the Thousand islands in the St. Lawrence river adjacent to the fine new international bridge that is being constructed there, and which will be opened in August. I cannot add much to what I have already said in that connection. The attraction in connection with the tourist traffic cannot be over-emphasized. A very large proportion of the population of the United States and Canada is situated within three hundred miles of this bridge, which will be about eight miles long from one bridgehead to the other. In that eight miles is of course included a considerable mileage of highway, there being five or six spans in the bridge. Representations have been made to the minister, I know, from different sources in this connection, and the one thing I do urge upon him is prompt action in connection with the securing of Hill island as part of this park. It has been recommended that a number of other islands be secured also.
Who owns that island?

It is used as farm land. There are no very valuable houses on it; the assessment is low; the valuation cannot be very high, but in the meantime interests may be created, purchases may take place that will make the acquisition of that land a more expensive matter than at the present time. If this property is to be preserved from commercialization for undesirable purposes, this very beautiful bit of scenery in the heart of the Thousand islands, it is absolutely necessary that some action be taken, and I suggest that the minister consider the matter.
I am aware that in the main the policy of the department is that the provinces acquire the land to be used for national parks, and turn it over to the dominion, but a return was brought down showing that in several cases land has been expropriated directly by the dominion government for park purposes. This return is sessional paper No. 242, brought down on April 25, 1938. The question was whether the dominion government has purchased or acquired by expropriation any lands for public park purposes since the year 1900; if so, what lands were purchased, where they were located and what price or compensation was paid for them in each case. That return covers nearly two pages and shows that in a number of cases the government has expropriated land, thus making an exception to the general rule that the land must be acquired by the provinces 
and turned over to the dominion. Land has been acquired in the Riding Mountain park for that purpose. In Georgian bay twenty-nine islands were purchased at a cost of $30,000. Then in the same area, I think, there was an exchange of land for other land. Land was purchased for the national historic park area at Louisburg in Nova Scotia at a cost of $23,250. At Banff national park lands were acquired in exchange; at Buffalo park and Elk island land was purchased costing $4,000. Then in British Columbia, in the Kootenay district, land was expropriated, and in the St. Lawrence area islands have been acquired from the Indian department. I understand, and in fact I know, that the policy of the government has been that islands in the St. Lawrence are preserved for park purposes, and inasmuch as Hill island was originally, as I recall it, the property of the dominion and was sold by the dominion, possibly being Indian land, I suggest that there is perhaps a little additional obligation on the dominion to contribute to the establishment of this park.
The minister has promised to go with one or two of his colleagues in the near future and look over the situation. I hope when he does so he will be favourably impressed, and in the meantime I urge that he consider the wisdom, almost the necessity, of issuing notice of expropriation in connection with this one island. There is not so much hurry about the others, not so much danger that they may be commercialized or that values will increase by any transfers that may be made in the meantime anticipating that ultimately the government will acquire the land for park purposes.

The point my hon. friend raises is rather interesting. Of course the practice has been that in connection with what are really national park areas the provincial governments supply the land that is to be converted into the national parks. So far as I am aware there have been no exceptions to that rule in the strict sense. My hon. friend has cited some instances from a report brought down in the house earlier this session. In western Canada, for instance, I know of several parks that are under the administration of the national parks branch which really were secured as wild animal sanctuaries. For example, when the small herd of buffalo were brought back to Canada from Montana in order to preserve that distinctly national animal in this country, an area was set aside at Wainwright; but that was wholly a dominion government undertaking. Strictly speaking Wainwright, and Elk island as well, are not national parks in the

Supply-Northwest Territories
real sense of the word; rather they are sanctuaries for the perpetuation and maintenance of certain types of animals which otherwise might become extinct. I have not the particulars of the other cases at the moment, but probably some equally good explanation would be available as to why the federal government spent money to acquire either new areas or additions to existing parks. Some of these matters really had to do with Indian lands. I think.
If the principle were adopted in this particular case-and I am not urging this at the moment as a reason for saying "no" to my hon. friend's request-the question would be raised at once in other parts of Canada. For instance, at the present moment New Brunswick is studying the question of recommending a suitable area in that province to the general parks administration. A few years ago Nova Scotia spent a very considerable sum of money in acquiring an area which could be turned over for development as a national park, and I think we have to adhere pretty strictly to that principle. Under that rule in practice, quite obviously if the area to which my hon. friend refers is desirable for national park purposes it should be secured by the government of Ontario.
As my hon. friend probably knows, we have a number of islands in the St. Lawrence river at the present time, a dozen or so, which constitute a national park, and I understand the request to be that Hill island be secured and added to those we already have. I propose along with one or two of my colleagues, if I can induce them to go with me, to visit that district just as soon as we can get a little relaxation from the strenuous work of the house. It is my intention personally to examine the problems the hon. member has raised.

With further reference to the suggestion that the province should acquire land for this purpose, I wish to point out that a new highway is being constructed for a good many miles along the river front, leaving a narrow fringe of what is really park land between the highway and the river. I understand that the provincial government is going to acquire and set apart that fringe for just this very purpose, namely to prevent commercialization and the destruction of natural scenery. That would be the provincial contribution. Under these circumstances I believe I might very fairly urge that the dominion make a similar contribution.
The return to which I have referred reveals that fourteen islands in the St. Lawrence between Brockville and Kingston were acquired in 1904. There is an acreage shown 51952-1951
of 180-8, and an expropriation and purchase price of $9,150. I know these are the islands to which the minister refers as having been set apart for park purposes. Pavilions and small wharves have been established upon them; they are open and accessible to the public and are very much appreciated. A great number of people use them.
I find another item with respect to twenty-nine islands in Georgian bay, acquired in 1929. Those islands had an acreage of 2,959-47 and a purchase price of $30,205. I am not familiar with the Georgian bay islands, but I do know that the islands in the St. Lawrence are suitable only for park purposes. They are not game preserves, or anything of that kind, but are connected with the tourist business, a business which alf governments are seeking to promote and develop. The federal government has placed great emphasis upon the value of that business.	[DOT]
I am glad to learn the minister intends to make the trip in the near future, because I am sure nothing but a visit to the place will give him a proper conception of the situation. I trust when he does go and has an opportunity to review the whole situation he will be convinced that in the interests of the dominion, and following the precedent which has been set in other cases, there is justification for acquiring at least this one island. Representations have been made that many of the islands should be acquired, and that course is no doubt desirable; but for the present Hill island is the one which should be kept in mind. Steps should be taken to prevent an artificial increase in value between now and the time the government takes it over. I say that because I am sure some government will take it over.
While the general policy is that the province should provide park sites, this case is exceptional. We know that the St. Lawrence river is exceptional in that it is an international stream. The federal government has acquired islands in circumstances similar to these. I am informed the government of the United States is doing something along the same line-on the part of the highway which is in that country. Some of the islands desirable for the-same purpose are located in the United States.. I am assured that the proper authorities in that country are taking steps to establish these islands as national parks, and have indicated a willingness to cooperate with the dominion government in that connection.
I thank the minister for his promise to visit the area, and I am hopeful that when he does understand the whole situation he will -become convinced that while it may be
Supply-Northwest Territories

necessary to make an exception, action here similar to that taken in connection with other islands in the St. Lawrence and in Georgian bay would be justified.

I appreciate what the hon. member has said, and would add for the information of the committee that the islands to which he referred in the St. Lawrence river and in Georgian bay were held by the Indians, and in effect there were transfers from the Indians to a government department. They were not acquired from private interests, according to the advice I have received. I assure the hon. member I will give consideration to the representations he has made.
My only reason for making the statement was that in the return I find the expression " expropriation and purchase the word " purchase " is used.
Of course a sum of money had to be paid to the Indians.
Exactly, although I do mot know that that makes much difference.

The road at the east side of the Big Bend highway on the Columbia river was built by the dominion government because that road lay within the park. To what point is the public allowed to drive cars? Is the bridge erected at the north, where the Canoe river comes in?
Yes.
How far can the tourists drive north, across the river and then south?
I cannot give the precise distance.
About ninety miles.
I should think a tourist might go ten or fifteen miles.
More than that.
From the north?

From where the bridge
crosses the river at the extreme northern point. That is more or less a guess on my part. Part of the road which is under construction tourists are not encouraged to use. But I can assure the hon. member that from Donald to Canoe river the road is in first class condition. I have been over it myself. May I call the attention of the committee to the fact that we have before us the item respecting the administration of the Northwest Territories. There are several other items under which parks administration could be discussed.
(Mr. Stewart.]

Has the government
under consideration the addition of Cooking Lake forest reserve to the Elk Island national park?
I understand some discussion in that connection has taken place with the responsible minister in Alberta.

Item agreed to.
Eastern Arctic expedition, $27,000.

Perhaps the minister would
tell us what is to be done in the eastern Arctic?

This item concerns chiefly the Royal Canadian Mounted Police posts maintained in the far north to exercise our sovereignty over the country. The Hudson's Bay Company take in supplies to the eastern Arctic every year, and we have an arrangement with them whereby the supplies to be sent in for the mounted police, for hospitals, for scientific expeditions and scientific purposes, are carried on the Hudson's Bay Company's boat. The arrangement is one that we consider quite satisfactory for the government. This item is practically all for that purpose.

Would the minister give
the assurance that there is no effective challenge of Canada's sovereignty over that vast northern area? I ask the question because we frequently see in periodicals of other countries reference to expeditions, the language of which would indicate that they consider that territory as open, not attached to any country, whereas my understanding is that Canada claims full sovereignty over the area lying in the Arctic north of Canada. It is a subject that I think should not be allowed to drift, and a frank declaration from the minister now would not be harmful. I have no desire to criticize or to press the matter further than to request a statement from the minister.

I know of no challenge
that has been made to Canada's occupancy or ownership of the whole area lying to the north. Certainly when any person from any other country desires to fly over that area or visit it, the permission of the Canadian government is first asked. The principles upon which sovereignty has been claimed over the area in the remote north which may not have been visited by man, say between the northern shores of Baffin Land and the pole, have been fairly clearly established in international usage, and under those principles, according to the advice that is given to me, Canada's position in regard to this

Supply-Yukon-Administration
area can, I think, be regarded as secure. Certainly at the present time no challenge has been made so far as I am aware to our right of occupancy and ownership of the area in question.
Is Wrangel island in Canadian territory?

No, Wrangel island is
Russian territory.
We have admitted that?
I am advised that we never claimed it.

Would the
minister state whether any new occupancy is being entered upon by the northwest mounted police?

There is a police post at Craig harbour on Ellesmere island; Bache peninsula port was the most northerly that has been established, although they have been further north than that, I am advised, and planted a flag or erected a mound or something of the kind on that territory. I think our possession of the territory is pretty clearly established. We have some mounted police there; my colleague the Minister of Justice tells me that they always carry out their duties very thoroughly and completely, and I have no doubt that our interests are fully protected.
The point is whether you consider the occupation complete enough to justify yourself in the minds of other governments.

I think the fact that they apply to us for permission to go into or fly over the territory is a recognition of our sovereignty. When the Russian flyers, for example, came over the North Pole and succeeded in getting as far as California, and another expedition that was lost last August, I think it was, wished to fly over that territory, they applied in both cases to the Canadian government for permission, which I would consider a more or less formal recognition of our rights in this region.
Mr. TAYLOlR (Nanaimo): Do our friends to the south also ask the same privilege?
Oh, yes.

Is there not international recognition of the fact that we have a sort of sovereignty over the triangle bounded by the Alaska-Yukon line, continued to the pole, and then to the west coast of Greenland? Is not that internationally accepted?

Yes. What is known as the sector principle, in the determination of these areas is now very generally recognized, and on the basis of that principle as well our sovereignty extends right to the pole within the limits of the sector. My own view is that our supremacy there is established to a point where it could not be successfully challenged by any other country. I do not know that I can add anything further.

Item agreed to.
Government of the Yukon territory: administration, $48,000.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to embarrass the government or delay the estimates but I should like to seek information as to the method employed or that should be employed in connection with the proposed transfer of the Yukon to the British Columbia government. The correspondence was brought down in the house, and while I have not it before me at the moment my recollection is that it consisted of one or two quite casual letters between the premier of British Columbia and the minister, dealing with the matter very much along the line that might be followed by a man buying a city lot. One man asks the other how much he will pay for it, and the other man says that is not enough, then there were some negotiations, and finally they agreed to take over the Yukon, as I said, like a man buying a city lot. Is there no custom of law or comity of nations by which the people are consulted when their territory is handed over to another jurisdiction? I cannot find from my observation in British Columbia that the province wanted the Yukon, and there is considerable evidence that the Yukon does not want us. Are not the common people, who after all are the people concerned, to be consulted before anything like that goes through? What is the situation?

My hon. friend is aware that no transfer of the Yukon to British Columbia can take place without appropriate legislation by this parliament and appropriate legislation by the legislature of British Columbia. The matter is not terminated with the exchange of letters that was tabled in the house some time ago. As I recall now, and I think I am correct, the suggestion was made that the matter might rest until after the Rowell commission had reported. I do not recall whether it is in the correspondence or not. The premier of British Columbia has made the suggestion that British Columbia should be extended eastward to take in part of the present Mackenzie river basin. However, so

Supply-Yukon-Administration
far as the people being consulted is concerned, they would be consulted in the way that they are consulted in respect of any legislation passing through either this house or the legislature of British Columbia; that is, before the transfer could be effective, legislation would be required not only in the federal parliament but in the legislature of British Columbia.

There did not appear in the correspondence any evidence of consulting anybody. It cannot be sold off like a sack or a ton of coals. It was said, "For a fixed sum you can have the Yukon." There was no suggestion about any local jurisdiction in the Yukon, for instance. It seems as though two hon. members got together and the one sold the property and the other agreed to take it over for a lump sum.

I can assure my hon. friend that it was not so casual as that. The plain fact of the matter is, of course, that any arrangement which might be entered into between the federal government and the government of British Columbia could not be made effective until the appropriate legislation had been passed in both jurisdictions.
And would the Yukon council be consulted?
Not necessarily.
"Not necessarily"?
No.
Well then, where do the people's rights come in?
I beg the hon. member's pardon?
Where do the people's rights come in?
Well, that is a question. While my hon. friend says they might not be consulted-
The minister said that.

-I say that any representations made by the Yukon council or any other interest in the Yukon would be given full consideration. But if the hon. member meant his question to imply that their consent was necessary, then I say it would not be required.
I hope we won't wake up some morning and find you have traded off British Columbia to the States without our knowing anything about it.
I can assure my hon. friend that should there be any project of that kind he will have plenty of notice so that there will be opportunity to raise a protest.

Now that the question has been raised regarding even any remote consideration of the taking over or absorption of the Yukon into the province of British Columbia, I certainly wish to register a very strong protest against the matter being advanced to any great extent without its being fully discussed in parliament-I mean, in advance of legislation. Because if the government of the dominion and the government of British Columbia come to a definite understanding and each one presents a bill before its legislature, obviously the government stands or falls by the passage of that bill.
Hear, hear.

The whole subject then becomes merely a question of the government securing the support of its partisans in the House of Commons, which is an entirely wrong basis upon which a matter of this kind should be considered or discussed. I am disturbed by the answers the minister has given about the paucity of discussion or consultation; therefore, I wish to say a few words on the subject at this time.
In the first place the administration of the Yukon over the years, and certainly for a great many years past, has been marked by a degree of efficiency and economy which is highly commendable. In a sense it is a small thing for the dominion, and the department might conclude that if they could shuffle it off upon some other authority they would be pleased to do it. But that is not the way in which the matter should be approached. The fact remains that there has been effective, sane and economic administration of Yukon affairs. While it is remote, it is a part of the country which has very considerable significance. In the past it has produced much wealth, and as the years go by and the movement is northward, as all who are acquainted with western and indeed general Canadian problems expect it to be, the Yukon will become more and more important. Its wealth possibilities are considerable, and not only in respect of minerals. The experiments which are being carried on by the United States, although in their initial stages they may not be wholly successful, indicate the existence of other possibilities.
The other side of the picture is this: British Columbia is an exceedingly large province, and that section of it, constituting at least half, which lies north of the Canadian National Railway is very sparsely developed. It is now entering upon an era of development, and so far as the province is concerned it has a vast territory of new country where it can expand its energies, and its surplus wealth'

Supply-Yukon-Administration
if it has any, and its powers of administration. In my opinion there are no sound economic reasons for the amalgamation at the present time of the Yukon and British Columbia. The other side, the human side of the story, ought to be considered. In the last forty years or more there has grown up in the Yukon a population which, although small in comparison to the rest of the country, has its rights, its peculiar sentiments and attachments, and certainly should not be disturbed unless it so wishes. The opportunity of handing over a comparatively small responsibility, administratively speaking, to the province should not be a determining factor. The determining factors should be economic advantage, whether economies can be made, and most important of all whether the people of the Yukon themselves desire it.
The Yukon is not a burden upon this country. The idea that it is has, in my belief, no foundation. It has produced a tremendous amount of wealth and will produce a great deal more. May I add that the officials, not only those who are carrying on at this time but those who for many years back have been attached, here in Ottawa, to the Yukon administration, and Yukon councils past and present, deserve a measure of commendation for their administrative work.
It would be most unfortunate and unfair if the question should be approached in the way indicated in the correspondence cited by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).

I wish to thank the last speaker (Mr. Stevens) for his very kind words. Naturally this is a subject about which I feel very keenly, having resided in that territory for forty years this month. There has been, as the hon. member who last spoke pointed out, a mistaken idea that the Yukon has been a burden to this country. It is not so. I have seen year after year in the estimates certain parts of the expenses of British Columbia lumped in with the expenses of the Yukon-for instance, the telegraph line. The telegraph line in the Yukon begins midway between Atlin and White Horse, but we pay for the telegraph line in that vast hinterland of British Columbia. For the last forty years we in the Yukon have had almost no crime. People who come from the coast in British Columbia, reading their papers as they are published day after day, will see reports of horrible crimes committed by boys and girls ranging from twelve to twenty years. We have nothing of that sort in the Yukon. Our children are put to work. They have to work or they go hungry; that is all
there is to it. The boys and girls born in that country know that they have to work for their living, if they do nothing but shoot game in the winter for the family table. In that way they learn to be self-reliant. Those of us who are in the Yukon, if there were a thought of annexation with some province that carried itself, that was not head over heels in debt, might feel interested. But I should like to know what we have to gain when somebody comes and says, "We will take you over so that you can clear off part of our debt." You do not see that in ordinary business life and certainly we do not want it in the life of our great northern country.
We have no fault to find with government as it is carried on in the north. We have had no complaints since the early days when the Yukon was so far out of the world that people who went there thought that they could do almost anything. Government has been carried on decently and honestly and as economically as possible. In the early days we went in over the trail on foot. We climbed those mountains and came down the waters of the lakes and rivers and went down in small boats. We became self-reliant. We knew what it was to get along without many of the amenities of so-called civilized life, and our children who live there now, though they may have the benefit of electricity and running water, still know that they must carry on as their parents did if they wish to accomplish anything in life.
As I have said so many times before, if we are only let alone to work out our own salvation we shall be a credit to the government of Canada as we have been in the past. We shall take pride in our government, I do not care on which side it sits. We simply want to work out our own salvation with the very small amount of help that we have had for many years. Individually we may not care for those who are administering the territory at this time, or that time, or at some other time; but no matter what our personal feeling is I am free to stand here and say that as far as humanly possible the administration of the territory, whether under Liberal or under Conservative government, has been decent, fair, square and honest. All I ask of the government is that they allow it to remain so, and not to trade us to any province that is head over heels in debt.

What is the attitude of the dominion government, as the governmental body in charge of the Yukon, towards the proposal to build a highway from the state of Washington to Alaska?

Supply-Yukon-Administration

I do not know that we have any particular views on that question. It is regarded as a British Columbia matter. I suppose if British Columbia can borrow money, and wants to build a highway through the province with the cash it gets, that is its affair, and I do not think the federal government would have any right to intervene.
Would not the federal government have a right to intervene if the money were supplied by and in agreement with a foreign country?

I did not refer to money being supplied by a foreign country. I presume that if British Columbia borrowed money in a foreign country in the ordinary way it would be their money to do with as they pleased.
It would not be in the ordinary way.

What about the Yukon? The road would have to go through the Yukon, and so far as the Yukon is concerned that is of concern to the dominion government. What would be the attitude of the dominion government towards such a road being built through the Yukon?
If the British Columbia government wished to build a road through a small part of the Yukon to reach its ultimate end, I do not think any question would be raised about that.
Would the dominion government be willing to cooperate in the building of such a road through the Yukon?

That is a question of
government policy and I am sure my hon. friend does not expect me to reply to it.
The minister said he would be willing to allow British Columbia to build the road.

I said that if British
Columbia went into the money market and borrowed money to build a road from the southern to the northern boundary of the province, that would be British Columbia's affair, not ours.

Even if it were a military
road?

I cannot conceive why
British Columbia would be building a military road. They would be building what is termed the Alaska highway.

Can the minister conceive
why the Americans would want to build a military highway?

That is another question
upon which I have no opinion to express. It is a question of public policy which is not germane to the discussion of the estimate before us.

The sum and substance
of it is that so far as the Yukon's part in such a highway is concerned, the dominion knows nothing about the plan, has not had it under consideration, and has no ideas at all. Is that correct?

Speaking for myself, all
I know about the matter is what I have seen in the newspapers. I can assure my hon. friend that the federal government is not considering the expenditure involved in the building of a highway through British Columbia to the Yukon, or in the Yukon section of it, for that matter. If I were to hint at such a thing, even in the most remote manner, the Minister of Finance would demand my head on a charger at once; consequently I can assure the hon. gentleman that the government is not considering the possibility of embarking on that enterprise.

I was very much interested
in the remarks of the hon. member for the Yukon (Mrs. Black). When the matter was once up in the house before-it was in the house, not in committee-I expressed the hope that, the occasion being Mrs. Black's birthday, she would long live to represent the Yukon in this house, and I very much regret to hear that she has made up her mind that she will not sit for the Yukon after this parliamentary term. I hope that decision is not irrevocable.
The absorption of the Yukon territory by British Columbia is not a matter for British Columbia alone; it is a matter for all the provinces of Canada, and one that would have to be considered by the government of Canada in relation to all the provinces. When the two new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved out, they were carved out of public domain that belonged to the whole of Canada, and the development from east to west has come up to expectations so far as the problem of transportation through the provinces to the coast is concerned. When the Yukon is tired of governing itself it should have something to say about the matter. I would add that when the people there are tired of self-government they should hand back that territory to be part of the public domain of Canada. We in the mari-times were not adjacent to any of this territory in the west, formerly part of the federal domain, out of which the great provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved, or

Supply-Forest Services
the hinterland given to Ontario, or that strip of country extending up to Hudson bay given to Manitoba, or that country rich in timber and water powers, Ungava, given to the province of Quebec. We had to sit by and keep our hands in our pockets for fear that what little we had might be extracted at the same time. We do not desire a further condition of that kind to arise. We hope the hon. member for the Yukon will come back representing the Yukon. Let them hand the land back to Canada as part of the public domain, and then this parliament will decide what to do in the light of the respective interests of all the provinces.

Item agreed to.
Dominion forest service-general scientific, economic and administrative services, $131,660.
Why is there a large increase in this item?

Last year part of the expense under this vote was in special supple-mentaries; this year it is included in the main vote. The combined total last year was a little in excess of the amount in the main estimate which we are considering at the moment.

Has this forestry service any control over the forests of the provinces? For instance in connection with the importance of forests to the watersheds of the country, and the large depletion of pulp-wood in Ontario, is there any control over the cutting down of trees by the department, or over the export of raw pulpwood from Ontario?

The provinces control their resources and consequently control the timber. But there have been five areas set aside where forestry experimental work is carried on under this department. In addition certain national parks are of considerable area and contain substantial forests. However the forest resources of a commercial kind are in the main under the control of the provinces. I understand they are at liberty to permit the export of pulp made from the wood cut in these forests if they wish. As far as I am aware no restriction has been put upon them in that respect.
Can the minister tell the committee how long the pulpwood resources of Ontario will last at the present rate of depletion?
I am sorry I cannot give that information.

The Canada Year Book says that the depletion of the forests
of Canada is about four billion cubic feet per annum. Has the minister any idea what the annual increase is? Is it true that we are cutting down in Canada about seventy years' growth for every year's growth that we replace?

I do not know how accurate that estimate of annual depletion is. The total depletion each year, including that cut and that destroyed by fire and insects, and particularly the annual increment, are very difficult to determine.

Is it not very important to Canada to know with fair accuracy what the depletion of our pulpwood is? We have mills dependent on the supply; we are at present exporting raw pulpwood to the United States to be manufactured into paper in competition with that produced in this country. Is there no way we can find that out?

The total annual depletion, caused by cutting, fire and insects, and timber past maturity and merchantable condition through age, has been estimated at about 3,800 million cubic feet. I do not see here any estimate as to the annual increment.

Closely connected with the depletion of our forests is the effect upon our watersheds and navigable waters. Has the government no control of the forests in that regard? What cooperation is there between the dominion and the provinces with respect to fire prevention activities and generally in connection with the depletion of our forests?

There is no division of responsibility between the provincial and federal governments either for protection from fire or for protection of watersheds. The timber resources are under the control of the various provinces. We could not go to the provinces of Quebec or British Columbia and say to them: You must administer your forests in such and such fashion. That is outside of our power. As far as fire prevention is concerned the federal government has for several years made a study of fire hazards and the conditions under which the fire hazard increases in our forests. It has been a scientific study, and very useful results have been obtained; so useful, in fact, that the data gathered in this way through our forest experimental work has been made available to provincial governments and also to private companies operating timber limits for the purpose of manufacturing lumber, pulp or the like. In many cases they have
Supply-Forest Services

made practical use, with very beneficial results, of the data that we were able to supply as a result of the experimental work done in this way.
The general question raised by my hon. friend is of quite considerable importance. Without doubt there is much destruction by fire each year, and through publicity work of one kind and another we have endeavoured to impress upon the Canadian people the importance of guarding against forest fires. I think I am correct in saying that eighty per cent of the fires that destroy our forests have their origin in the carelessness of some human being. The only way to overcome that, I suppose, or at any rate one way to help overcome it, is by impressing upon the people in every way possible the importance of exercising care if they are travelling through the woods; if they are camping, or if their activities are such that they may be the means of starting a fire in our forests. All that work we are endeavouring to do. We give a grant, as will be noted under a later item, for the purpose of spreading popular education through the Canadian Forestry Association. It is only a small amount, but that association derives some of its support from private sources. In all these ways our department is doing what it can not only to aid the industry but also to create that wider public opinion that will have its effect in lowering the percentage of fires that have their origin in carelessness.

Cooperation between the federal and provincial governments is most important. There should be strict cooperation among the provinces as well. A fire starting on the border of Ontario might well go into Quebec, so that the closest cooperation is necessary. If it is left a purely provincial matter as between Ontario and Quebec there is a possibility that it might not be taken as seriously by one province as by another; but I congratulate the minister on what has been done.
I should like to ask one more question, with respect to pulpwood. Is it within the competence of the dominion government to prohibit the export of raw pulpwood from Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: An order in council was passed in 1924, I think, prohibiting the export of pulpwood from private lands; of course we cannot prohibit the export from provincial crown lands. I am not quite sure whether the order in council was ever proclaimed, but as far as I know certainly this house has full authority to prohibit the exportation of pulpwood or logs from private lands.

I think that information should be given more publicity, because in British Columbia there has been considerable agitation to stop the export of logs from that province; and in debating the question many people hold the belief that it is a matter for the dominion government. Our information this afternoon is that the province of Quebec has the power to prohibit the export of logs and pulpwood, and if that is so I see no reason why British Columbia should not have the same right.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Since 1906, there has been a prohibition of the exportation of pulpwood cut from crown lands in the province of Quebec, and that order in council is still in force and effect.

I should like to draw the attention of the government to the necessity of preserving the pulpwood limits of Canada for the benefit of Canadians. I do not think very much benefit accrues to the individual Canadian by the cutting down of a tree and the shipping of that tree to some other country. I should like the government to look into the question whether or not they have the right to prohibit the export of raw pulpwood from Canada.
I should like to ask another question while I am on my feet. Could the minister tell me the present status of the forest experiment stations, at Petawawa, Kananaskis, Duck Mountain, Valcartier, and the Acadian, the one at Fredericton.
I do not think I quite get the point of my hon. friend's question. Did he ask what is the status of each of these experimental stations?
Yes. As the minister knows, the dominion government owns certain lands on which experimentation had been carried on. Is that work being continued and, if so, to what extent, or has it been dropped?

The work is being carried on at each of these experimental stations. Naturally the conditions in Manitoba vary considerably from the conditions in Ontario. There are different types of trees and so on, and these stations were established originally with the idea of conducting a study that would not overlap as between stations but that would fit together to give a general picture of the value of our forest woods, the best methods of protection, the rapidity of growth under varying conditions, and like matters. That is the type of work that is being carried on at each of these forest experimental stations. The data is gathered

Supply-Forest Services
together and compared, and from it very useful conclusions can be drawn. I understand that in some cases these conclusions have had practical value and are being applied by the forest woods industry in its various branches in Canada. These stations vary in size, Petawawa I think being the largest. The one at Petawawa is roughly one hundred square miles; the one at Kananaskis in Alberta is sixty-seven square miles, and the Acadian station in New Brunswick is seventy square miles. The others are smaller.

The work being done in connection with these experiments is indeed excellent and I should not like to see any lessening of efforts in this direction. I trust the department will bend its efforts towards increasing the work, in view of the depletion of Canada's forests.

Reverting to the question of the export of logs from crown granted lands, I sincerely hope the government and the minister will pay earnest attention to this serious matter. In British Columbia the situation is urgent. The period of availability of logs and timber generally is not more than fifteen years. An extended availability does not exceed twenty-five years. In view of the fact that public opinion in British Columbia is being very strongly awakened, and the further fact that the federal government does have some responsibility and has acknowledged its power to prohibit the export of logs, it seems to me the matter should be taken in hand very early. I say that because one of the greatest areas in British Columbia, one no less than forty square miles in extent is being logged by Japanese loggers for Japanese owners, for purposes of export to Japan. Even from the standpoint of a consideration of the preservation of our own resources the matter merits the earnest consideration of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When the question was discussed a few moments ago it occurred to me that perhaps the discussion was a little in reverse. As to the federal powers in connection with controlling the export of any commodity in Canada, wherever or however produced, I suppose one might say that in this parliament there is no doubt we could make general laws covering the export of any commodity. I am not a constitutional lawyer, but I doubt whether any province could deal with the export of a commodity. But, owning the lands upon which the timber grows, the province sets the conditions of cutting, and of course in setting the conditions of cutting in its own judgment it can determine whether or
not the timber cut from lands owned by the crown in the right of the province shall be used for this or that purpose. That could be a condition precedent to any extension of the cutting right.
But when we come to privately owned lands -I believe it was these the Minister of Pensions and National Health had in mind-and whether under the circumstances the province could impose on those private lands cutting conditions which would have the same effect with respect to exportation as would conditions set by the province with respect to cutting on crown lands, I think we get into a rather involved constitutional question. The matter is of course one of some difficulty, but this parliament acting for the country generally has not yet, so far as I know placed an embargo on the export of any commercial commodity. There is the question whether any laws affecting the export of commodities could apply nationally with respect to a commodity which came from a particular place, as distinct from the same commodity which came from another place; because the dominion's power undoubtedly is exercisable with regard to the commodity as such. To identify a particular log as having originated in a particular place, or to attempt to apply to lumber which is exported from one part of Canada export regulations which would not apply equally to lumber exported from another part of Canada, or to go further and to consider applying export regulations with respect to commodities destined to a particular foreign country as distinct from export generally, are all very involved questions of constitutional and international law, and of trade generally.

I thank the Minister of Finance for his explanation. It was the observations of the Minister of Pensions and National Health which brought me to my feet. I quite agree with what the Minister of Finance has said: the question whether or not we have any power to place an embargo upon the export of privately owned material is an involved one. But the question arises: Are those materials more necessary for the people of Canada than for people outside Canada? It was a consideration of that question which prompted me to make my observations. I do not agree with the procedure of enforcing embargoes; I believe free manufacturers and free producers have a right to export, and in that I respect the statement of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, may I point out that the export of pulpwood and logs has an effect on the watersheds and navigable waters of the country. There is no doubt that if the forests become depleted the waters in the navigable streams under the control of the federal government will be lowered. We can see that happening in Canada at the present time. No doubt the export of forest products must in some degree lower the waters in the St. Lawrence waterway system from lake Superior to the ocean. It seems to me the federal government should take under advisement the question of the lowered water levels and the depletion of the forests.

It is not the export of pulpwood or logs but rather the cutting and removal of those logs from the land which affects the water or climatic conditions in an area. The export of the forest products to a profitable market does not injure the coverage of the soil to any greater degree than it would be injured if those forest products were sold less profitably at home. The greatest damage is done by fire, which destroys not only the useful pulpwood logs and timber suitable for lumber but also the weed growth and the less valuable trees. I suggest the export of logs and pulpwood need not be considered in connection with the preservation of watersheds.

I notice the present estimates call for an expenditure of $359,300 for forestry projects. While there is some increase over the amount voted last year, to my mind the sum is most inadequate, having regard not only to the direct value of the forest industry to the country but also to the indirect value for the conservation of water and wild life, the attraction of tourists, and the availability to our people of a free means of healthy recreation.
