Mr. PURD\ : I think the direct value of the forests and forest industries of Canada are well summed up in the closing paragraphs of a book recently published by the Department of Mines and Resources, entitled, Economic Aspects of the Forests and Forest Industries of Canada. The summary is on page 53 and reads as follows:
The products of the forests and forest industries provided the largest favourable balance in external commodity trade during the period 1931-35, and stood second in this respect to agricultural and vegetable products in 1936.
The United States and the United Kingdom are Canada's best customers for forest products, and also supply the larger part of her import requirements.
Of the total volume of wood taken from the forests from 1931 to 1935, over 92 per cent was either consumed in Canada or subjected to further manufacturing processes before being exported.
I draw that to the attention of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) who has spoken of wood products being exported in the raw state. I continue the quotation:
The estimated net average value of forest products consumed annually during the same period was 132 million dollars, which included imports valued at approximately 14 million dollars. The value of Canadian products consumed at home was, therefore, 118 million dollars, and the additions to the wealth of Canada, accruing from forests and forest industries, averaged 275 million dollars annually.
From the same publication I observe that 13-8 per cent of the total car loadings of Canada originate with this industry, and therefore it has a very important bearing on the income of our railroads. I would suggest to hon. members who have not already obtained a copy of this publication that they do so, because it is of exceptional interest.
There is another important fact brought out in this book which would seem to substantiate my claim for further consideration for the industry, and that is that approximately one-fifth of the value of the primary production of Canada originates in the forests. I suggest that that is a very modest estimate because I observe from the last issue of The National Revenue Review that of our total exports of Canadian produce in April 1938. amounting to $51,248,752, a total of $11,668,934 came from this industry.
I quite appreciate the fact that in most of the provinces a large percentage of the forest lands is still owned by the crown in the right of the provinces. But the situation in the province of Nova Scotia is entirely reversed, and 87-6 per cent is owned by private parties. It is with privately owned lands in Nova Scotia that I would like to deal for a few moments.

Supply-Forest Services
I would first like to point out that some 40,000 of our farms consist in part of cleared land and in part of wood lots, and I would throw out the suggestion to the government that in these wood lots, and in other wood lots privately owned, they have an opportunity of doing for Nova Scotia what they have done and are endeavouring to do for the west in the matter of agriculture. If the west is adapted to the growing of grain, then surely we in Nova Scotia can say with equal truth that our land is adapted to the growing of timber, and claim equal recognition and consideration on this ground. Nova Scotia spruce, pine, birch and maple are by-words in the markets of the British Isles and also of the United States, and if this government would take steps to maintain and increase the supply of these woods it would go a long way towards rehabilitating the rural sections of this province.
With no. portion of our province more than thirty miles from tidewater and none of our land inaccessible for operating purposes, it will easily be seen that having regard to the increasing demand for these products from abroad, the expenditure of moneys for the development of forests in the province of Nova Scotia would give a greater return than in any of the others. In addition I think it is recognized that on account of climatic conditions tree growth is more rapid there than in most other places in Canada.
For the year 1937 it is estimated that in addition to firewood the products of our forests and forest industries were in excess of the equivalent of 500,000,000 feet board measure. While accurate figures are not available it is conceded from all sides that this cut was greater than the natural increase and that if we were to continue at that rate for many years our forests would be depleted.
On the other side of the picture, however, we have between twelve and fifteen thousand square miles of timber land or land suitable for growing timber. Experience has shown that under natural conditions many lots which were cropped forty years ago or less have in the past few years produced a crop of from 4,000 to 5,000 board feet per acre, and in many cases far in excess of this.
It seems to me that with proper care and study we have sufficient land in the province to give us an annual cut in excess of the figure named above, and it is toward this end that I would urge on the government the necessity and advisability, as a first step of the establishment of an experimental forest station in this province. Or perhaps a series of demonstration stations would be more
suitable, so that the farmers of the various districts could be educated to look upon their wood lots as a portion of their farms the same as they do their cultivated lands, harvesting each year only the trees ready to be cut and improving the growth of the remainder by scientific methods.
Full utilization of the waste products of the industry now destroyed or left to decay could in my opinion, with some assistance, be made to give gainful employment to a large number of our present unemployed.
I shall not further take the time of the committee to enlarge on the subject or to point out the many advantages that would accrue if these schemes could be worked out. I sincerely trust, however, that the minister will give the matter his careful consideration, and I can assure him that he and his officers will receive full cooperation from the provincial department.
Another point I would like to stress in favour of growing timber instead of growing grain, is that if the demand is poor, cutting can be curtailed with benefits to the stands, whereas in agriculture this is not possible. Further, when the time comes for the selection of sites for these experimental stations and the minister sends his officials to Nova Scotia, I trust that they will not overlook the constituency of Colchester-Hants, which is the biggest lumber producing constituency in the province.

I will certainly give consideration to the representations my hon. friend has made. I might mention that Cape Breton Island park is now under development, covering an area of five hundred square miles, and we have under consideration making some study within the park area of the timber growth and other resources relating thereto.
Mr. PUiRDY: The minister's officials, when they visit Cape Breton national park, will find that the woods there are entirely different from the growth on the mainland, and that the land within the park is not very well suited to the production of useful timber.
I am glad to have that suggestion from my hon. friend.

Item agreed to.
Forest experiment stations, $77,520.

I presume I am the only one who attempts to criticize increases in estimates. I should like a little information on the reason for this one. It seems to be the government's policy that all estimates shall be increased. Here we have increases in this department, following the many in-
Supply-Forest Services

creases that were made in the Department of Agriculture. Why almost $36,000 should be added to the expenditure on forest experiment stations I cannot understand. This is no time for increasing experiments. Money should not be spent to-day unless it will bring work and wages to the unemployed. But this is pure experimental work, and I suggest that the government do not waste $36,000 more on experiments of this kind.

I might make to the hon. member the same remark I made to the committee on an earlier vote. In last year's estimates, with which he makes a comparison, he is dealing only with the main estimates; and if we take the total spent last year in main and special supplementaries, and set that against the amount in this vote, this vote is actually less than it was a year ago.
Your, estimates do not show it this year.
I know, but if we take into account the special supplementaries voted last year-
Oh, well, I do not have them here.

I notice that the hon. member for Melfort is not in the house; but in answer to what he said, I should like to remark that the necessity of keeping our pulpwood and manufacturing paper in this country and not exporting it, is that we have in the pulp and paper industry an investment of some $175,728,000, and it is necessary to keep the supplies for those mills in Canada. We can manufacture it here just as well as they can in the United States, and with more benefit to Canadians.

Item agreed to.
Forest Products Laboratories, $148,500.

We should like to hear what the minister has to say about this; what are the laboratories doing? The minister is probably familiar with the laboratory at Madison, Wisconsin, where wonderful work along this line is being done. I should like to know what work is being done in Canada in this respect, and upon what all this money is being spent.
There are three of these laboratories. One in Vancouver, one in Ottawa, and one in Montreal.
What are they associated with?

The study of the utilization of forest products. For instance, studies are 
being conducted as to the strength of woods, how woods can be most economically used, for example, in various building materials. Then there is the study of the utilization of waste material from wood, such things as sawdust and bark and slabs, which a few years ago were considered as waste material altogether; also, the study of lumber seasoning ; how our forest products can be best manufactured to suit the markets to which they may be going. These matters are studied particularly at the Vancouver and Ottawa stations. The Montreal laboratory is devoted almost entirely to the pulp and paper business which forms such a large and important part of the industry in both Quebec and Ontario. Scientific experiments are carried on with a view to the improvement of the quality of the paper by treatment of pulp. All that sort of thing is carried on in Montreal, and the department has had a definite recognition from the pulp and paper industry of the value of the government's contribution to this laboratory. I might say, as was pointed out in discussions of similar estimates in previous years, that the Montreal laboratory was begun through the cooperation of McGill university, the pulp and paper industry, and the federal government. To the costs of operating this particular laboratory the pulp and paper association make a contribution, in addition to that which comes from the federal government.
Is there a revenue from it?
No. You do not derive much direct revenue from experimental stations.
This is not an experimental station. This is a laboratory.
Well, I mean from laboratories.

The United States government receives considerable revenue from a similar line of work at its great laboratory at Madison, Wisconsin. When that laboratory renders a service along the lines the minister has outlined, and along scores and hundreds of other lines, it makes a charge for it. All that the minister has said is very largely the sort of information which has been handed down from the research bureau here, so that if these experimental stations are doing the same work, that is, only a duplication of what is being done here, then what is the research bureau doing?

The research bureau is not doing research work in this particular field.

Supply-Forest Services
That is being done by the laboratory at Montreal. The same applies to the forest laboratories at Ottawa and Vancouver. That field is not being duplicated by the national research council.

Do they also inquire into the proper kind of wood or lumber to be used for shipping purposes, for crating and so forth, so as to advise manufacturers of the strength of certain kinds of wood for certain lines of shipments, whereby they are able to reduce the weight and thus reduce the freight charges?

Those matters are studied not only in the Ottawa station but in the Vancouver station as well. Studies are also made of the lasting qualities of various kinds of woods, and what treatments can be given them to increase their length of usefulness. All these matters, which are purely scientific, are under investigation at both Ottawa and Vancouver. As I stated a moment ago, the Montreal establishment confines its activities very largely to those problems which relate to the pulp and paper industry in Canada.
How much was expended last year on the Vancouver laboratory?

The vote this year is divided as follows:	To Vancouver, 834,572;
to Montreal, $38,829; and to Ottawa, $75,099.

The minister said that experiments were carried on in connection with waste material such as slabs, sawdust and so forth. What has been the result of those experiments? Is there any result from them so far?

I cannot say that so
ar there have been any practical results.

How long have they been
carrying on these experiments?

I am informed that it
is only within the last year that work of this kind has been undertaken.

Are there any
field research units associated with these laboratories, outdoors?
The officers in these various laboratories go out and have contacts with the people who are actually in the industry. Jf that is what my hon. friend means, the answer is yes.

Not exactly.
What I am trying to discover is whether any of these departments are directing themselves to the comparative advantages of natural or ordered reafforestation.

That comes under the
various experimental stations. It is not related to the work under this particular vote.
Is anything being done in that direction?

Yes. A study is being
made at these various experimental stations. There is one in New Brunswick, one at Val-cartier, one at Petawawa, one in Manitoba and one in Alberta. Experimental work is carried on as to the rate of tree growth, the conditions under which growth is best promoted, the matter of fire hazard and how it can best be provided against, and so on. All these matters are under constant study at these experimental stations. For instance, plots will be thinned down to a certain number of trees per acre to ascertain the relative rate of growth as compared with a stand which is much thicker. In a general way the work carried on is directed as far as possible to wholly practical ends, and when the data is accumulated it is passed on to those engaged in the industry in various parts of Canada. As I said earlier, we have had from people engaged in various branches of the woods industry commendations regarding the practical value they have received from the work carried on at these stations.

Where is the laboratory
in British Columbia located?

In the university grounds
in Vancouver.
What varieties of timber of economic value are found in Alberta, and for what purposes are they used?

We have no laboratory in Alberta. Conditions in the three western provinces are fairly similar so far as the type of timber produced is concerned. There is. of course, an experimental station at Kanan-askis, but there is no laboratory.

Item agreed to.
Grant to Canadian forestry association, $1,620.
What are the objects of this organization, and what has it done?

It was initiated under prviate enterprise to bring home more clearly to the Canadian people the value of the forests and the need of fire protection; in short, to develop a sort of forest consciousness in the people. It has largely been supported by private effort, and grants have been given for a considerable number of years, not only as a recognition of the useful work that the association is doing but as a practical aid in carrying it on.
Supply-Ordnance Lands

Perhaps hon. members have not been sufficiently impressed with the serious depletion of the forests on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains in Alberta, and the effect which this may have on the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We are going forward with a prairie farm rehabilitation scheme which, I am sure, will be extended as the years go by, the object being to bring under irrigation a large part of what is now semi-arid land. The water with which these projects will be carried on must come from the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. It happens that some of them are in my constituency and others in Macleod riding, and therefore I am familiar with them. There is grave danger of forest fires crossing the mountains and destroying these forests. Such a thing has happened many times. I am informed that there is scarcely sufficient forest supervision to ensure ability to stop a fire soon enough to prevent a disaster. I understand that it takes about one hundred years for a burned forest to be replenished. These facts are sufficiently serious to make us stop and think. It would be far wiser to spend some extra money in protecting the forests as they are now, and some money in encouraging reafforestation so as to preserve the water, before it is too late. The Saskatchewan river, the South Saskatchewan particularly, and other great rivers flowing down the eastern slopes depend largely upon forests for their water. There is a genuine problem there. At present the task of looking after these forests is in the hands of the province.
They own and control them.

I realize they do. but in these times when the provinces are in such straitened circumstances financially it would seem the part of wisdom for the dominion to make sure that there shall be no lack of adequate forest supervision. I emphasize this because, if these forests are destroyed and that water supply is in considerable degree diminished, it will long be a matter for regret; for it will be a loss that we shall not be able to replace.

Item agreed to.
Land registry: Land registry, seed grain collections, administration of ordnance, admiralty and public lands, $64,000.
It seems a curious thing to mix up seed grain collections with administration of ordnance lands.

It arises from what is left of the land administration of the old Department of the Interior. This land registry has several activities. It is responsible for the

administration of federal lands reserved under the natural resources agreement; it has the handling of military reserves that may have been abandoned for that purpose, of the issue of letters patent for lands in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and the administration of ordnance and admiralty lands on the east and west coasts and also on the great lakes. There are still some remnants of those old lands. Generally speaking, it is an office of record for all the lands controlled by or under the federal administration. It is a sort of omnibus item carrying everything that could not be attached anywhere else.
From whom are the seed grain collections made?

On advances made many years ago, some as far back as 1914, I think, in the prairie provinces. My officers tell me it goes back as far as 1876; I do not think there are many of those, but some old claims date back to 1914. They are endeavouring to collect these; in some instances compromises are reached on the amounts.

Item agreed to.
To provide for expenses in connection with the determination of boundaries of ordnance and admiralty lands in the province of British Columbia, $3,000.

This is an item which
has been in the estimates for a good many years. We have not been able to make much progress with the British Columbia government in getting the matter actively in hand to have the boundaries of some of these lands delimited, but we may be able to make some progress this year.
How many pieces are there in British Columbia?
About fifty, I understand.

Why only in British
Columbia?

I understand this arises
out of some provision in the act transferring the Peace River block and the railway belt to British Columbia. Provision was made then for the settlement of these boundaries. I am told that in some instances Indian reserves are involved. The matter has been under discussion with the British Columbia government; but they and the department here have never been able to agree on it, although it has been under discussion for several years.

Can the minister hold out any hope that they will ever get the matter of the Indian reserves in British Columbia settled, concerning which there was an agree-

Supply-Labour
ment made, known, I think, as the McKenna agreement, which originated about 1918? I know a large, expensive delegation went about British Columbia and made arrangements to cut off land from some large reserves not needing it and add land to others; the province agreed to surrender those lands necessary to be surrendered by it, and the dominion agreed to reciprocate, but as far as I know the matter has never been settled. There seems to be an almost childish sort of dispute in connection with some of the terms. If the matter has been settled, I should be glad to know, and, if so, when the settlement was reached. The delay is holding up a lot of progress that might be made. Parts of these reserves could be sold to public advantage, but sale cannot be carried out because no one has a title; the dominion does not have it because the province will not sign, and the province is still retaining it under a sort of pledge to give it to the dominion.

The matter is now under negotiation with the British Columbia government. Various efforts have been made to settle it, but without avail. I personally discussed the matter with the premier of British Columbia on his recent visit to Ottawa, and urged that it should be settled.
What is the trouble?

It is hard for me to say. Apparently there is in British Columbia some official view held rather strongly on the question. But I believe there is no good reason why it should not be settled. The basis of settlement was agreed upon. I urged upon the premier of British Columbia that it should have the immediate and careful consideration of his government, and he assured me it would be taken in hand. I hope when we come to consideration of these estimates a year hence the committee can be given the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move that the committee rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again this day, in order to permit of the tabling of the supplementary estimates, and also a statement of the Minister of Labour in connection therewith, the intention being to ask the Speaker to leave the chair immediately after the message of his excellency has been received, and to call an item in the Department of Labour.

A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the 51952-196
financial year ending March 31, 1939, was presented by Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance), and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister
of Finance) moved:
That the message of His Excellency, together with the supplementary estimates presented this day, be referred to the committee of supply, with the exception of items Nos. 633, 634 and 635, which I would ask the house to refer to the standing commitee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government.

Would the minister kindly explain his reference just now to the fact that it was the desire of the government to call an item under the Department of Labour. Surely that is quite an unusual thing to do, with the supplementaries laid before the house now for the first time.

speechtext: I am sorry; I thought I had made that clear. I am sorry I did not make that clear previously.
Labour has been called already?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Motion agreed to.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

International Labour Conference, $15,000.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Chairman, in view of the questions raised during the recent debate on unemployment, I believe it will meet the wishes of the committee if a brief statement is made at this time with respect to the supplementary estimates which have just been tabled.
In these estimates provision is made for work-creating projects amounting to a total expenditure of over $40,000,000. This is in addition to work-creating projects in the main estimates amounting to an almost equal sum. Apart from expenditures on public buildings in the various provinces and the normal outlay for the repair of wharves and breakwaters, the larger items in these estimates
Supply-Labour

carry out the policy of the government to stimulate basic industries and broaden the foundations of a long range program of conservation and development. An amount of $1,310,000 is set aside for improved road transportation into new mining areas, and there is a further supplementary vote for geological surveys, in addition to the $300,000 appearing in the main estimates. The total of proposed expenditures on highway improvements apart from mining roads is over $3,500,000. Of this total there is a new item of $1,000,000 to reduce the menace of level crossings as a supplement to the contribution of $500,000 to the grade crossing fund already made in the main estimates. Over $3,000,000 is assigned to trans-Canada and tourist highways and national parks. Another item in the group of expenditures designed to assist the tourist industry is the sum of $450,000 for the restoration and development of historic sites.
Over $7,000,000 is to be spent on special projects of harbour and river development, including a contribution of $300,000 to the Grand River conservation project in Ontario. There are substantial construction outlays for harbour improvements at Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and Vancouver.
The sum of $1,000,000 is also to be spent on canal improvements in addition to the expenditures appearing in the main estimates.
The sum of $650,000 is to be spent for the encouragement of the fishing industry.
The expansion of facilities for air transportation is given a prominent place in the development program. The sum of $800,000 is allocated for the construction and improvement of airports along the trans-Canada route and an additional $500,000 for assistance to municipal airports. This is in addition to the sum, in the main estimates, of $1,722,400 for the construction of airports, and $800,000 for assistance to municipal airports.
As announced in the speech from the throne the youth training plans are to be extended. The sum of $2,250,000 is included in the estimates for training projects for unemployed young people and older unemployed persons. A considerable portion of this amount will be used for forestry training and conservation.
To provide for rehabilitation and water storage in the prairie provinces under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act the sum of $3,500,000 is included in the supplementary estimates. This amount will be expended largely in the drought areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

New expenditures are included for forest conservation and fur conservation.
It is also possible at this time to make a further announcement which, I believe, will be welcomed in the house and in the country. In accordance with the principles laid down in the recommendations of the national employment commission, legislation will be introduced at the present session to provide additional encouragement to low cost and low rental housing. Legislation will also be introduced to provide low interest loans to municipalities for self-liquidating projects. These important developments of the government's program are designed to give further stimulus to the construction industry and to provide additional employment through private and public enterprise in large centres of population and in localities which may not benefit directly from the construction of public buildings and other works projects.

May I ask the
minister one question? Until these projects get under way, has the government made any provision for the emergency situation that prevails in Vancouver, Calgary, Winnipeg, Windsor and, in fact, nearly all our larger centres, where there are large numbers, especially of single men, who are not to-day provided for?

Although the supplementary estimates remain to be passed providing for grants in aid to the provinces, those provinces concerned have the assurance that when the grants in aid are passed they will be made retroactive to cover the months since the expiration of the last fiscal year. There has been a difficult situation in Vancouver during the past few weeks. As I have stated before in the house, the government of British Columbia has been dealing with the situation in consultation with the Department of Labour here, and of course I am aware of the measures that have been taken in that province to deal with the immediate situation. As far as the other cities mentioned by my hon. friend are concerned, I know of no emergency situation which is not being met in the ordinary way through the provision of direct relief or in such other ways as have been employed by the provincial governments for that purpose.

I wonder if the minister would go a little more fully into the Vancouver and British Columbia situation. I notice by this morning's newspapers that the minister of labour of British Columbia made the statement that 1,800 single men who came into the province at the end of last year were to be returned to the provinces

Supply-Labour
in which they may have domiciles, and that if they did not accept that offer they would receive no more relief. From the same press dispatches I understand that the western cities or other provinces to which they are to be returned are objecting to that being done. Are any steps being taken to ensure that if these men are compelled to leave British Columbia, they will be maintained in the other provinces to which they may be sent or to which they wish to go?

I should be inclined to answer that question in this way: The men to whom my hon. friend has referred received employment in forestry conservation camps during the winter months. The dominion government contributed to the maintenance of those camps, which were carried on cooperatively by the dominion and provincial governments. These men received wages at the prevailing rate of thirty cents an hour while they were in the camps, and a portion of their pay was deferred and made payable to them after they loft the camps, in the form of post office vouchers. Had these men who came from other provinces chosen to return to those provinces at the conclusion of the work in the forestry camps, no possible objection could have been taken by the authorities in the provinces from which they had come originally. That, as I understand it, is what is now proposed by the provincial government; that these men who came to these forestry camps from other provinces shall be granted transportation to their homes. I have the assurance that in determining the destinations of these men to whom transportation will be given every possible safeguard is taken to see that they are sent to their own homes, or, in other words, to the places from which they came to enter the forestry camps in British Columbia during the past winter. As a matter of fact, my information also states that of those who have applied for transportation almost all have indicated as their homes smaller centres of population in the prairie provinces. So that up to this time we have no indication that there is likely to be a large concentration in the cities of western Canada. The number mentioned by the hon. member is also, I believe, something in excess of the actual number who would qualify for transportation under the plan proposed by the minister of labour of British Columbia.
No doubt the minister has seen the press dispatches and realizes I mentioned the number indicated in those dispatches.
Quite.

Are those the steps to which the minister referred when he said the provincial government had taken steps to deal with the situation? I ask that because I have understood that there were several thousand men assembled in Vancouver and the shipping back of 1,800 or 1,900 of them still leaves a large number in that city who will have to be cared for by the citizens. For instance, last Saturday a tag day was held at which the sum of $4,000 or $5,000 was raised. To a certain extent by threatening the city permission was obtained to hold the tag day. Is it the intention to reopen the forestry camps until these works projects are started, or is the government taking any other steps in the interim to meet the situation.

The government of British Columbia in dealing with this situation at close range-not a new situation entirely, but something which has developed from time to time in recent years-has decided it will be possible to absorb in employment in the province those who were formerly in the forestry conservation camps and who were residents of British Columbia. As a matter of fact, the experience of last year suggests that this has been done. About 2,500 men who were in the forestry camps of British Columbia last winter did not return this winter. The clear inference is that they had either found employment elsewhere or returned to their homes in the prairie provinces. As I have said, the province of British Columbia is able to judge as to the best measures with which to deal with the existing situation. As I understand the situation, it is not the intention to open forestry camps.
As the minister must know, there is far less employment in the woods of British Columbia this year than last; that will mean less opportunity to place these men.

I am not able to give a definite opinion on that point. I have understood that there was a certain slackening in the forest operations in certain parts of British Columbia, but within the last few days I have heard evidence to the contrary. At all events, the statement made by the minister in the British Columbia government suggests that in his belief it will be possible to find employment for those formerly in the camps and properly resident in the province.

The minister is satisfied that the difficulty has been settled in the coast cities, then?
Private Bills

Mr. ROGERS r I am afraid I am never Satisfied that difficulties of this kind are Settled. To some extent they ar.. chronic, and inherent in the problem with which the country and government is dealing at the present time; but I believe I can say-and perhaps this is known to members of the house-that many of those young men were induced to remain in Vancouver. They are organized in the relief project workers union, and I believe the efforts of the leaders in that union were directed toward dissuading those young men from returning to their own homes when work in the forestry camps was ended.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, May 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain).
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, 1 believe the hi inis ter of Transport (Mr. Howe) was speaking at the expiry of the hour for public and private bills when this motion was last before the house. He is unable to be present to-night, and has requested me to say to the house on his behalf what he would have said had he been able to be here and conclude his remarks.
The Minister of Transport says that when he last discussed this bill he had arrived at the point of making some remarks on the major contention of the member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) to the effect that mill feeds should move from the mills to consumers in British Columbia at rates now applicable to feed grain. The minister had pointed out that the hon. member for New Westminster was in error in stating that such a movement now takes place on a domestic rate for milling grain, as in fact the movement is now carried out on the balance of the through rate from the point at which the grain itself originates, and this balance of the through rate is usually lower than the domestic grain rate, and often as low as or lower than the rate on feed grain.
The Minister of Transport has conferred with both railways on the matter of the contention of the hon. member for New Westminster and has pointed out to them that a grievance, although the railways claim it is not a very real one, is still a grievance and should be removed by every means consistent with maintaining a reasonable rate structure. The railways are disposed to accept the minister's view of the situation, and after giving the matter full consideration both railways have authorized the Minister of Transport to

Railway Act-Grain Rates
make the following statement, which in his opinion concedes the demand of the hon. member for New Westminster and those who support his view so far as rates on mill feeds are concerned. The following is the statement of the railways handed to the Minister of Transport:
The railways will make provision in their tariffs that on straight carload lots of feed forwarded from the milling point, the balance of the rate as applicable under the railway regular milling and transit arrangements will not be in excess of the feed grain rates from the milling point. The railways will also provide in their tariffs applicable on feed grains that the rates named therein will apply on straight carloads of mill feeds from specific points at which mills are located in Alberta and Saskatchewan to points in British Columbia. The above special rates will be withdrawn if it forces reductions generally on feeds between points in western Canada.
The Minister of Transport states that it is only fair to point out once again that the present rates on feed grain were agreed to by the railways with the understanding that they represented a compromise between the demands of the four western provinces and the then existing tariffs. It is the minister's understanding that this compromise was accepted by each of the four western provinces, and having accepted the compromise, the minister doubts the propriety of further demands within the previous settlement. It is now the opinion of the Minister of Transport that the fact that both railways are willing to introduce the new rate voluntarily should be accepted as an indication of the desire of the railways to meet the needs of the agricultural development of British Columbia, and the minister suggests to the hon. member for New Westminster that he should withdraw this bill with the understanding that the new tariffs on mill feeds will be published without delay.
The minister desires to point out to members of the house that the very low rates now applicable on natural products moving for export are made possible only by a reasonable balance between export traffic and the movement of more valuable commodities within Canada. Truck competition has made heavy inroads on that kind of traffic, while drought conditions have reduced the export volume of grain. These two situations combine to create Canada's railway problem. The railways have every desire to meet the needs of agriculture. Ton mile rates in Canada for the products of the farm are far lower than for parallel lines in the United States, and are in fact the lowest rates in the world. While moving traffic at these rates, we expect our railways to produce a balanced budget, and the Minister of Transport suggests that we should not ask the
impossible in further reduction of rates that are now well below the cost of the service given.
Western Canada has always been ably represented on the board of railway commissioners, and the minister believes that no one can claim that the railway board has not understood the needs of western Canada and given sympathetic consideration to those needs.
In conclusion, the Minister of Transport desires to state again that parliament has constituted the board of railway commissioners the final authority to adjudicate on railway rates, and he expresses the hope that in future members of the house will address matters of rate adjustment to the board of railway commissioners rather than to parliament itself.
That is the end of the statement, Mr. Speaker, which the Minister of Transport desired me to make on his behalf.
On my own behalf may I say that I have a vivid recollection, going back through the years, of the continuous struggle in connection with this matter of westbound rates on feed grains. In fact, my recollection goes back vividly to the original fights with respect to-the Crowsnest rates eastbound, of which it might be said that the bills introduced year after year by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) have been a by-product. I think all of us would agree in principle that parliament, having delegated the responsibility for rate making to the board of railway commissioners, should not, unless under exceptional circumstances, constitute itself the judge as to what a given freight rate should be on any commodity between points in any part of Canada. I speak, of course, subject to the fact that certain statutory rates enacted by this parliament before the board was created: do exist and have been a ruling factor in relation to the commodities and the geographical' areas with which they deal, even though the board has since come into existence for the purpose of regulating rates generally in Canada. I hope that the hon. member for New" Westminster will regard the further concession which the railways have authorized the Minister of Transport to offer as sufficient warrant to justify him in withdrawing the measurer which is now before the house. By so doing, we shall avoid further parliamentary adjudication with respect to railway rate matters, which, as I have said, all of us regard as undesirable generally. .Of course parliament is the highest court in the land, and there is no means of preventing discussion of these matters in parliament, nor is there any desire on the part of anyone to prevent such discussion. Nevertheless, parliament having created a

body and clothed it with the necessary authority, it is desirable, generally speaking, that that body should be left as free as possible in order that it may exercise its jurisdiction equitably on behalf of the people of Canada whom it is appointed to serve.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF CROW'SNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext:
The decision of the government, as indicated in the statement read by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), is an extraordinary one. I agree with the minister and have always held that the question of fixing rates ought to be left to the railway board. The first speech which I made in this house, in the autumn of 1911, was on that subject, when the late Mr. MacLean, from Toronto, introduced a resolution calling upon parliament to take some action with regard to fixing rates. I then took the ground I did because I had faith in the railway board as an institution. I believe that the board, on the whole, has been one of the fairest courts in the land. It is, of course, more a court of equity than a court of law. It has earned for itself a record of justice and fairness, and in the choice of its chairmen the country has been singularly fortunate. I appeared before it years ago, when the late Mr. Justice Mabee was the presiding official, and before him Mr. Justice Killam, as well as those who have followed. In all instances, I believe, the gentlemen who have been the chairmen of the board have been distinguished by their fairness and their sense of equity. Therefore I have never felt comfortable when these bills were brought before parliament. It is true that on certain rare occasions when freight rates have been discussed, I have taken a stand in the house in regard to them, but in my opinion it has been more or less unfortunate that they should have been introduced into this house.
Having said that, I confess to a considerable disturbance of mind in witnessing a government-to judge from the document which was read-actually having discussed the matter and brought pressure upon railways in order to overcome an inconvenient measure which was brought before the house by one of its supporters. I suppose we might liken the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) to the importunate widow who by her persistent attempts at last won some attention.

I do not object to the effect of it, but I object to the form of it.
Here is another consideration. The hon. member upon one or two occasions has appealed to the governor general in council, as was his right. I believe it would have been far better for the governor general in council, in accordance with the law, to take some action on appeal from the board of railway commissioners, than to have the matter dragged into the house and made more or less a political football, because that is what it amounts to. It will be quoted in the country as evidence of what can be done in parliament by anyone who wishes to be persistent and, shall I say, sufficiently embarrassing to the government. In my opinion it is an unfortunate precedent that the government should have given way, although in the concluding remarks of the minister's statement he made a pious appeal to all hon. members that in future they would be good boys and not embarrass the government in this way any more, but leave the subject to the board of railway commissioners. The rates should have been granted before or, they should not be granted to-day; the rates should have been granted by the board of railway commissioners or, on appeal, action should have been taken by the governor general in council. I am not condemning the hon. member for his action, other than to say this, that I do not agree with this form of rate making. In his desire to gratify his ambitions he has a perfect right to embarrass the government he is supporting; but it is a poor line of business and an unfortunate precedent to establish in the house that if an hon. member can make himself enough of a nuisance to the government in some way or another, he will get his wishes and his demands gratified.

I have always held that it is better to leave matters to courts that are set up to deal with them than to bring them here. What I am deploring is not this particular incident but the fact that a concession should have been granted in this way. It should have been done by the governor general in council upon appeal from the board of railway commissioners. That is the proper way, and if the government had decided to follow that course it would have been better to invite the hon. member to reopen his appeal before the governor general in council and have action taken in that way.
It is not adding either to the dignity of, or to public confidence in, the board of railway commissioners. Here are two railways coming and saying, "We have been harassed about this matter, and now we shall give so much if you will withdraw the bill and not bother us about the rest." In the statement read a few minutes ago they intimate that the moment there is any agitation in the territory with respect to intervening points they will withdraw this concession. The whole thing is on the basis of logrolling, whereas it should be on the footing of the findings of a court of equity and should stand as a matter of justice. It should be a matter of justice, or it should not be done at all. Either the rates are justified or they are not, and the board should be behind them.
This board is at the present time in a state of transition. Under the transport act it is going to become the board of transport and to it are to be handed enlarged powers to administer not only the railways but waterborne traffic, air traffic and other matters. In other words, the powers and jurisdiction of the board are to be extended; but just at the time of transition we find the board, a court which as I say has earned for itself a right to the confidence of the country, being brushed aside and a set of rates fixed
by a log-rolling process. It is that feature of the matter to which I object. I suppose the hon. member who introduced the bill and who has been so assiduous in his advocacy of it in the house, where a good many of us feel it should not be, will receive some encomiums for having achieved a great victory. I do not believe, however, that victories of that kind should be achieved in this house at the expense of constitutional and proper methods and at the expense, further, of public confidence in our judiciary, because if you are going to do this sort of thing in this instance you might just as well do it in some other matter.
All the talk about this being the high court of parliament, this high-sounding phrase, makes me a little weary. If there is a body in this country less fitted to be a court, it is this house, and we might as well admit it.

Unfortunately, even the proper and legitimate functions of parliament are not discharged in the best possible form because of the introduction of patronage which has grown up over the years. Courts have been established and the confidence of the people has reposed in those courts. That confidence should not under any circumstances be disturbed. If there is one thing that we should be proud of in Canada, it is the respect which, down through' the decades, the people have had for the courts of the land, and unfortunately these are times when loosely expressed opinions have a tendency to disturb the confidence of the less informed people of the country in our courts. Railway Act-Grain Rates

I have not time to go into all the matters 1 should like to deal with, because I do not want to be accused again of talking out my own bill. The railways require traffic these days, and I know of no better way to get it than by encouraging the movement of grain to British Columbia so that the poultry-men and dairymen of that province may produce more eggs, poultry, butter and cream. We have lost a great market in the old country; we are sending only one-half of one per cent of their total requirements in eggs. The British market takes 240,000,000 dozen eggs a year, but last year Canada only supplied approximately one and a half million dozen. In 1928 the railways received $298,000 in freight on eggs alone leaving the province of British Columbia for other markets, whereas last year they received only a total of some $7,000. In 1927 the number of laying poultry in British Columbia amounted to 2,750,205, whereas in 1936 the number had dropped to less than 1,500,000. In 1927 we produced 27,500,000 dozen eggs, whereas in 1936, the latest year for which I have the figures, the number had dropped to 15,800,000 dozen.
I should like to mention one point here. Perhaps this -may be not pertinent to the discussion on my bill, but I believe it should be brought to the attention of the house. British Columbia is bringing in this year, and brought in last year, many bushels of wheat. They brought it from Yakimo, a distance of 634 miles, to Cloverdale, near my own home town, at the rate of 34 cents per 100 pounds. That comprised No. 2 and No. 3 grades of wheat. And, note that it was brought in from across the line. We might also commence to grow in the province of British Columbia, and particularly in the Fraser valley, hard wheat. In my own constituency we have the world's champion grower of hard wheat who won the Chicago world's championship last year. The gentleman's name is Mr. W. G. Gibson, and I have a sample of his wheat in my hand. It is called Reward, and those who have sampled or looked at it, including the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), believe it is harder than the wheat grown on the prairies. Bear in mind that this wheat was grown at sea level, right at the coast, and that-is something unprecedented in wheat production. I think it is only right and fair that some honourable recognition be given to the man who produced this fine quality of hard wheat, Mr. Gibson of Ladner.
Mr. Speaker, my time is passing, and I should like to conclude what I have to say.

Yes; you are now at your
usual interjecting. No matter what claims have been made by Conservative members in connection with the rates given on feed grain by the railways in 1933, I maintain that the bill introduced by myself had considerable effect on what was done in that year. My bill had to be voted on, whereas the resolution of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was disposed of by being adjourned or talked out, and was therefore not so embarrassing to the government.
It got results, though.

It was a concession to my
bill, and has saved the people of British Columbia a considerable sum of money. Mill feeds might also have been included in the same manner, had the then Minister of Railways demanded that they be put in the agreement. The proposal to include now mill feeds and carry them at the same freight rate as feed grain, while it is not as much as the people of British Columbia would like to obtain, still it is a considerable concession, and I believe it would be much better to accept what has been offered than to refuse the bill altogether. As mill feed constitutes fifty per cent of the feed requirements of the poultrymen and dairymen of British Columbia, the proposal will mean an annual saving of approximately $100,000. I am disposed tonight to accept that proposal. It will also mean a saving of around $5,000 annually to the members of Fraser Valley Surrey Farmers' Cooperative Association. It will certainly mean a considerable saving to the 600 members of that association.
It has been a long battle to obtain what has been accomplished, but I believe the fight has been a worth while effort on behalf of the people of the province. I wish to say tonight that in agreeing to withdraw the bill I am not agreeing to discontinue the fight.
I am willing to accept half a loaf, so to speak, in the belief that it is better than no bread. The saving of $100,000 annually is certainly, I must say, a worth while concession in the meantime. But even that is not what the people of British Columbia want.
Had I had time I should have liked to go into the loss to the railways. It has been pointed out that the freight rates in the United States are higher than those in Canada. I should like time to meet that argument, because I dispute the statement to that effect made by the Minister of Transport. May I give one instance of what is taking place right now, to show where we are losing a great deal of trade because of high rates in

Supply-Lands, Parks and Forests
Canada. I have before me an invoice of a piano shipped from Toronto to Vancouver. That piano weighing 550 pounds was sent at the regular freight rates, and the freight bill amounted to $33. The same company brought a grand piano from the same point, namely Toronto, shipped it by way of Chicago and Seattle, then completed the shipment by reshipping by regular freight rates to Vancouver. The grand piano weighed 700 pounds, or 150 pounds more than the other, but it was carried the whole distance at a cost of $19, as against $33 over the Canadian route.
I have in mind another case which will perhaps be known to the hon. member for Fraser Valley. The greatest rose grower in British Columbia, Mr. H. M. Eddie, possibly the greatest in Canada, who lives in the constituency the hon. member represents, wanted to ship rose bushes from that point to eastern Canada, and particularly to Toronto. He was quoted a rate of $3.58 per 100 pounds by the Canadian railways, and the United States railways quoted a rate of $1.58 for the same distance. The United States railway landed them in Toronto at that rate and in about the same time. I mention these facts to show that it is about time we reconstructed the rate structure, and had something more in keeping with the times.
I am sorry I have not more time to develop further arguments, because I had much more to say, but I realize it is almost nine o'clock and I am afraid that again I might be accused of talking out my bill.
Is it the pleasure of the house that the hon. member have leave to withdraw his bill?
No.
Carried.
The bill will be withdrawn.
