The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Lands, parks and forests branch-To provide for expenses in connection with the determination of boundaries of ordnance and admiralty lands in the province of British Columbia, $3,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we were
considering this item when my progress in connection with the estimates was interrupted. I had given an explanation of the item.

I think I was asking the minister with regard to the location of these lands, and he had said that the delineation of boundaries was an old matter. I wonder where the difficulty lies in connection with boundary delineation? There must be some plans. Is there difficulty in connection with actually laying them out on the ground?

I am informed that the procedure involves a search of old records and old titles that are in the records office of the legislature of British Columbia. Altogether there are now fifty parcels; originally there were 170 parcels.
In British Columbia?

In British Columbia
altogether, and there are about fifty of them left. We hope to make some progress with the matter this year; in fact, we had hoped to make some progress last year and did not, and consequently we have this item in the estimates again this year to cover the expenses deemed necessary in clearing the matter up. I hope I may be able to report to the house next year, if I am still responsible for this department, that the matter has been disposed of.

The statement just made by the minister brings up a question about which I had a word or two to say last year. The minister has told us that originally there were over a hundred parcels in British Columbia, and that now there are approximately only fifty. Evidently some of them have been disposed of in the meantime. I know that in Ontario applications have been made from time to time to the department for the purchase of some of these ordnance lands which lie along the shores of the great lakes, and the minister was quite firm at that time that there was no chance and no inclination on the part of the government to dispose of any of these lands. In Ontario there have been disputes over the boundary lines because these lines lie adjacent to farmers' property. Whether these ordnance lands have been encroached upon or whether the boundaries have never been clearly established I cannot say, but I would ask the minister why, if ordnance lands have been disposed of in British Columbia, it is impossible for applications for ordnance lands in Ontario to be granted at any time.

Supply-Lands, Parks and Forests
These were disposed of in British Columbia years ago. I am not at the moment familiar with any difficulty in Ontario.
I do not know that at the moment there is any difficulty over boundary lines.

My information is that there is not; but these cases in British Columbia are still outstanding, and we think their land department has been rather dilatory in doing its part. Perhaps this may be regarded as unfair criticism. I do not so intend it. As I have said before, I discussed this matter with the premier of British Columbia when he was here recently, and we hope to make some progress this year.
Does the minister expect eventually to dispose of these lands, or is this merely for the delineation of the boundaries?

This is to get the boundaries determined and the titles cleared up. After that, the question of what might be done with these lands will be considered. There will also be the question, I am advised, of their need or suitability for defence purposes. But the problem at the moment is to get the boundaries and the titles cleared up.
Is some of it city property?

I am advised that none of these lands is in that category now. There were some in the past but the province disposed of them, but the titles to these parcels have yet to be fully cleared up. Quite frankly, I think it is a matter that should have been settled years ago.

My reason for speaking on this item, Mr. Chairman, is that along the north shore of lake Erie and lake Ontario, but lake Erie particularly, there is a number of summer cottages strung all the way along the lake shore, and in many places there is ordnance property which would make an excellent site for a summer cottage, but the department in the last few years has consistently refused to make any arrangements for the sale or transfer of these properties. My idea was that in case of war or these properties being needed by the government for some purpose, they could be expropriated if necessary, but in the meantime they are lying idle and are overgrown with weeds which are more or less a menace to the neighbourhood. It would be much better if the department would take into consideration

the disposal of such of these properties as are not necessary for ordnance or defence purposes.
I shall be veiy glad to take the suggestion of my hon. friend into consideration. At the moment there are no questions at issue so far as I know.
I have had applications, not this last year, but within the last two or three or four years, from people who were anxious to purchase and were unable to do so.

We are not selling ordnance lands, and that has been the policy not only of this government but, I think, of preceding governments; but I am advised that a lease may be granted on these lands, and I suppose that applications for the lease of some particular piece of property for the erection of a cottage or for some other purpose would be considered. My hon. friend says he made reference to the question last year, but this is really the first I have heard of it. There is in regard to these ordnance lands in Ontario no difficulty such as I mentioned in connection with the lands in British Columbia.

My only reason for mentioning the matter was that the minister had said that there had been over one hundred parcels of these ordnance lands in British Columbia, and now there were only fifty. I supposed some had been disposed of, and I wondered why one province was being treated differently from another.

There has been no change in the situation in British Columbia for many years. These lands originated, I dare say, even before the provincial government was formed, away back in the time of Governor Douglas in British Columbia. The matter has dragged along and really should be cleared up. I do not know that I can add anything further.

Would the minister tell u? if the title to the foreshore of navigable rivers is vested in the federal government or in the province, and is there any difference between such lands in front of municipalities and those in front of unorganized territory? To be more explicit, take the Columbia river, which is a navigable stream. In which government is the title to these foreshores vested?

That lies wholly, I think, with the province of British Columbia. The Columbia river flows through that province; they own the land on either side of the river and, I think, the foreshore rights as well.

Supply-National Parks
Frankly, I am not familiar with the legal position of the matter. But my information now is, and certainly my impression is, that in the case cited by the hon. member the foreshore rights would lie with the province of British Columbia.
Does the riparian owner not own out to the middle of the stream or creek or river?

Yes; I should think probably he would. I do not know whether that answers the point raised by my hon. friend. If a riparian owner has bought a river lot in British Columbia, I suppose under provincial law that would carry certain rights out to the middle of the stream, but the authority to dispose of that lies, and has lain in the past, with the province.

Item agreed to.
National parks bureau-National parks and historic sites services, $1,383,500.

This is a general item dealing with the administration of all the national parks in Canada. There are now altogether about twenty of these national parks established, embracing an area of roughly
12,500	square miles. The purpose of this vote is to pay for the administration costs of the parks, and improvements within the parks such as maintenance of roads and, in some instances, the construction of new roads. The increase as indicated in the estimates arises in the same way as one or two other increases I referred to earlier on other items: that is, we have included in the estimates this year for national parks considerable sums which heretofore were either in special supplemen-taries or, under the late administration, under the Public Works Construction Act. After we combine all the figures there is an actual decrease in the vote as compared with a year ago. That, of course, does not include the supplementary estimates which were tabled this afternoon.
Would the minister give us the number of historic sites? He mentioned the number of parks. I imagine that will include the historic sites as well.

I find in the report of the lands, parks and forests branch for the year ended March 31, 1937, that at the close of the fiscal year 1936-37 a total of 239 sites of national importance in Canada had been acquired by the department. Of this number 235 have been marked by the erection of suitable memorials on the recommendation of the historic sites and monuments board of Canada.
Is that pamphlet available for anyone who desires it?

Oh, yes. It is an annual report of the lands, parks and forests branch. It is incorporated in the report of the Department of Mines and Resources. There is a great deal of useful information in that report.

When can the minister give any information about the Garibaldi park area near the city of Vancouver, British Columbia? I understand that area was offered to the federal government for a national park some seven or eight years ago. Has it been accepted as a national park area?

No. Garibaldi park is, I understand, a provincial park under the control of the provincial government. Suggestions have been made that it might be taken over by the federal government and incorporated in the national parks of Canada. It is an interesting suggestion, and some day, probably, it will be acted upon. But, after all, in the development of national parks we have to cut our coat according to the measure of our cloth. The decision was reached a few years ago to establish a national park in Nova Scotia, and development in that park is taking place now. Prior to that, parks were established in Manitoba, and in Saskatchewan north of Prince Albert, within the last ten years. The development of national parks is progressive. Obviously, as I stated a moment ago, we must have regard to the amount of money we have available to spend for this purpose. I should say that some time in the future-I am not going to predict when- the Garibaldi park proposition might be considered. I know the view is held, particularly in Vancouver, that Garibaldi park would be a desirable acquisition for the national parks system of the dominion. But according to our information quite a considerable amount of money would be needed to make any appreciable development in the park, principally in the way of constructing roads to it, as well as carrying on other necessary developments. At the moment we are not in a position to undertake that development.

I quite understand that the government could not take over and develop all the land which might be available for national parks in the dominion, and that development must necessarily be fairly slow, but I believe there are, in connection with this area, circumstances that the government should take into consideration in the very near future. The late Doctor Tolmie, when he was premier of British Columbia,
Supply-National Parks

definitely offered the area to the federal government to be developed as a national park. It is one of extremely fine scenic beauty, and it is only about fifty miles from Vancouver. As a tourist attraction so close to the largest city in British Columbia, I do not suppose there is anything else to equal it. I hope the minister's department will give consideration to it, as there is a strong desiie in British Columbia, and particularly, as the minister himself said, in Vancouver, to have this area opened up as a park.

We shall be glad indeed to give consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend. I might point out to the committee, though, that there are already four national parks in British Columbia: Kootenay park, the Yoho, Glacier, and the park at Revelstoke. These embrace altogether an area of about 1,700 square miles. And we have requests for the establishment of national parks in provinces in which there are not any. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) was urging this afternoon consideration of the establishment of a national park in the area along the St. Lawrence river below Kingston. Well, Ontario has a few, small national parks. There is a small park at Point Pelee, which is the most southerly point in Canada on lake Erie, and there are the islands in Georgian bay which belonged originally to the Indians and were secured from them many years ago for national park purposes, and the islands in the St. Lawrence river. Quebec has not yet a national park, although the Quebec government has broached the question of establishing one. New Brunswick has not yet a park, although the matter of selecting a site is under consideration. When there are four national parks already established in British Columbia and none in some of the other provinces, my hon. friend will appreciate some of the difficulties that we would face if we attempted to ignore New Brunswick, for instance, or Quebec, and proceeded to establish a fifth park in British Columbia. I know that he will appreciate the problem which would face the administration in that respect and I hope he will sympathize with me.

I suppose the reason why
the department cannot assume responsibility for developing Garibaldi as a national park is not merely the fact that there are already some other parks in British' Columbia, but that the limit of the financial resources allowed by the government to the department has been reached. May I take this opportunity to direct the attention of the department to two matters. In the first place, I would point out that the parks in

the Rocky mountain and Selkirk mountain areas were never developed as British Columbia parks. They grew out of a great conception that Sir William Van Home had that those parks would be a real asset to the Canadian Pacific railway, and then the idea was copied into Jasper park, not as a. British Columbia park but as a park that would be a real acquisition in the development of traffic for the railways. The fact is that there are no national parks in British Columbia in the sense that national parks are established in other places.
With regard to the question of finance, it seems more than strange that, when we realize that through national parks can be sold to the greatest advantage Canada's chief export asset, namely her tourist trade attractions, some recognition of the tourist trade of Canada is not given in appropriating moneys for the development of further tourist trade attractions. The figures indicate that out of a total revenue of some $300,000,000 from tourist trade there is an actual profit to the dominion of somewhere between $160,000,000 and $180,000,000. I venture to say that this favourable balance, which is so essential to a nation carrying so heavy a load of foreign debt, would not exist at all if it were not for the park facilities and the natural attractions that Canada enjoys at the present time.
There can be no good reason why a nation that enjoys a revenue of $300,000,000 a year from the tourist trade cannot appropriate to the development of national parks and of highways leading to them, the funds that are necessary to make them as attractive as possible. As a matter of fact, the policy which is being pursued here is one that is probably costing the dominion anywhere from $200,000,000 to $500,000,000 a year, because it is a policy which persistently refuses to recognize the fact that Canadian credit can be properly and safely invested in the development of those Canadian assets which will increase foreign revenue and develop revenues from abroad. I happen to be interested in Garibaldi park because it affects, by reason of its lack of development, the economic life of the city of Vancouver and of a substantial portion of British Columbia. Today, for want of the kind of attraction that Garibaldi would offer, thousands upon thousands of Canadians from Vancouver and British Columbia generally are now going across the boundary line and finding that entertainment both in summer and in winter in the great parks of Mount Baker and Mount Rainier in Washington. That drift southward will show, I think, that British Columbia of all the provinces of Canada has an adverse

Supply-National Parks
balance of tourist trade. I am confident that, if Garibaldi park were opened and developed as it could be, instead of Canadians going south by thousands they would find better entertainment in that park than they can get elsewhere, and because of that thousands upon thousands of United States citizens would come north where we to-day are going south.
There is another reason why Garibaldi should be developed. The government, quite wisely I think, has recognized the fact that to serve the 130,000,000 people in the south who own and operate some 28,000,000 automobiles, it is good business for the administration to cooperate in building highways through gateway points into various sections of the dominion. If we could get a highway connection from the boundary line at Blaine, through Vancouver, across the First Narrows bridge now being built by private capital, and up Howe sound to Garibaldi park, recognizing that as the first link in the Alaska highway from the southern boundary line, we could show the government a possible revenue in tolls if it were necessary, and certainly in the way of tourists from the south, which would make it a good, sound, self-liquidating investment and turn an adverse balance of trade into a favourable one. I should like the minister to take up the question with his colleagues, and particularly the Minister of Finance, and ascertain why it is that this nation of ours, richer in proportion to its population than any other nation in the world, cannot find the means to develop those attractions which are essential to the advancement of our international trade. Why is it that nations like Germany and Italy can find money without limit to finance an aggressive program of armament, while we Canadians cannot find a few million dollars for the development of our national parks and roads? There is no good reason why any Canadian should look either to the soviets or to Germany or Italy for lessons in finance. Let us forget the dictatorships and ascertain from our own Department of Finance why it is that Great Britain, hopelessly bankrupt in 1931, to-day can stand forth and meet the threats of almost the whole world ranged against her and finance a great program of social reconstruction, of rehousing, of national defence, carrying her obligations clear out to the enormous Singapore base in the far east. If the 45,000,000 English people can do what they are doing, why have we to stand shivering in impotence, unable to develop assets like Garibaldi park in British Columbia, which are just as necessary in the interests of Canada and of every province from ocean to ocean?
The time may soon come when we in Canada must look at what is going on elsewhere in the world, and particularly in Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand. Our Canadian people are not going to remain satisfied with answers such as we have had to-night. With our government in possession of all this wealth, boasting of a favourable trade balance of hundreds of millions of dollars, of a favourable balance from tourist trade last year of $160,000,000 odd, and more this year, I am satisfied that our Canadian people will not accept as reasonable the statement that we have not the money to put our unemployed men, who are ready and anxious lor employment, to work in developing the kind of thing that experience and records of performance prove will pay and pay well. We have no reason to be afraid of the future, unless those in the seats of government have lost confidence in the possibility of future development of this nation's wealth. If the government lose faith in the nation, it is impossible to expect others to have confidence.
But I do congratulate the Department of Mines and Resources upon the splendid work it has been doing and the splendid results it has achieved. I venture to say that, of all the things accomplished, the opening up of roads and trails and the development of highways from the international boundary to our national parks has given the best kind of employment and been probably the best practical service, not only in eliminating immediate unemployment but in removing unemployment as a continuing evil, of any step this government has taken. My hope i3 that, in view of the splendid results which have been achieved, those of us who have faith in the great program the minister is carrying out will rally to his support and do all we can to guide the Department of Finance out of that swamp of financial ignorance in which it seems to be lost.
How much of the roads in the Banff national park and the Waterton lakes national park is hard surfaced?
So far we have no hardsurfaced roads within these park boundaries.
I would not criticize the type of roads that are in the two parks I have mentioned. I have been over nearly every road in the Banff national park except the one now being constructed up to Jasper-
Do not miss that; that is the best.

I hope it will be. The roads are in good condition; but there are, and will be every year, spots in them that

Supply-National Parks

need considerable repair, because notwithstanding the fact that the roads are graveled and well scraped and oiled, they do deteriorate. There was a time when tourists and citizens going into those parks used to talk about the terrible roads until one got to the gates of the parks, and then one could depend upon the roads being good. But now the picture has to some extent changed. As far as the Alberta side of those two parks is concerned

and some credit is coming to this government for the assistance they have given-the road from Calgary into the Banff park is now hard surfaced and is a splendid road. When you come to the gate of the park the road is fair to good, but not hard surfaced. If you are going into the Waterton lakes park from the east or northeast, the road is now hard surfaced from Macleod into Pincher Creek; from Pincher Creek on the road is fair but not hard surfaced.
Following the remarks of the last speaker concerning the tourist trade, I suggest to the minister that I believe no better circle tour could be found, from the many points of view I have in mind, than the one from Calgary through to Banff and down the Windermere highway, and return by way of Macleod and Lethbridge. You can take a number of side roads if you wish; but the route I have in mind is through to Cranbrook, east through the Crowsnest pass, visiting the Waterton lakes national park, then up to Macleod or through by Cardston and Lethbridge and back to Calgary. I believe that is one of the most wonderful tours in Canada, from the standpoint both of scenic beauty and of what one might learn of the wealth and industry in different parts of this territory. From Calgary west through the Cochrane district there is a most wonderful ranching country, with eighty or ninety miles of good, hard-surfaced road. We know what is at Banff; that has been well advertised, and I shall have something to say in that connection later on. The road through the Banff national park and down the Windermere highway certainly is beautiful, and I want to compliment the minister upon the continual improvements that are being made in various projects within the park. Then, coming through the Crowsnest pass, we get a glimpse of the coal mining industry of Alberta. It is in the mountains, but tourists are interested in other things than scenery. If you go through to Pincher Creek, down to Waterton Park and back again either by way of Macleod or through Cardston and Raymond, you go through a magnificent stretch of farming country. I would even 
go so far as to mention that it has been said that the Mormon temple at Cardston is one of the unique buildings in the British Empire. Certainly it is a point of interest. Then there is the Raymond sugar factory, which is another point of interest, as well as all those irrigation projects in and around that district. If one wanted to take a little side trip from Lethbridge into the Taber district he would see a canning factory, and it is no little two by four factory. They can put out vast quantities of fruit and vegetables from that place. If you go north towards Calgary again, whether you take the route by way of Macleod or by way of Lethbridge, you will go through one of the greatest wheat growing areas you could find anywhere. It has been said that in the Champion-Vulcan district, and to the north, as much wheat can be produced from a given area as can be produced anywhere in the world. Of course, in the last few years we have experienced a good deal of drought there, but in good years, Mr. Chairman, we can certainly grow wheat. In Vulcan, which is a small village, there are nine large elevators. In Nanton, which is about the same size, I think there are about nine elevators also. I should not forget to mention that before entering Calgary you can go through the famous Turner valley oil fields. That is a sight to behold, a sight that any tourist coming to Canada will love to see. This is a circle tour within which you find all these points of interest.
I should like to say another word in this connection. I have not received a copy of the supplementary estimates, but I notice the Evening Citizen mentions that in them $40,000,000 is provided for public works. Perhaps we can discuss that at another time; but I would say to the minister, and to the Minister of Labour, that there could be no more profitable project undertaken in Canada than to see that the highways in that circle tour are hard surfaced. I realize that this is partly a provincial responsibility; but if the sum of $40,000,000 is to spent on public works in an attempt to put the unemployed to work, I believe the government would be well advised to spend some of the money right there. They would get it back in a few years, through the tourist trade that would come to this country.
I should also like to compliment the minister upon that project in the Banff national park known as the "Cascade of Time." I fancy that project comes under this department rather than under the town of Banff. Of course, at the present time it is not much more than a beautiful garden; but a good deal

Supply-National Parks
of work is being done on it from year to year, and certainly it is becoming a real beauty spot.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to ask the minister if he is able to give the committee any information as to whether or not some of the money that is to be spent for public works-I am talking now of the $40,000,000-will be spent on the roads I have mentioned. Would the minister care to make a pronouncement on that point? I know it is pretty early to say very much about it.

No; at the moment I am not in a position to make any definite statement in that regard; but doubtless my hon. friend will get the information in good time, when the supplementary estimates are under consideration. This year we are planning to do some hard surfacing in Banff, and also to carry on with the work that has been in progress for a few years now, designed to create a hard-surfaced highway from Kings-gate north to Cranbrook and into the park system at Radium Hot Springs, then out to Calgary, over the road my hon. friend has mentioned; from Calgary south to Waterton lakes and on to the Glacier national park in the United States. We are making progress with that. I quite realize the importance of the point raised by my hon. friend as to the value of hard-surfaced roads for tourist traffic; I think there is an increasing realization of the importance of such roads. I have no doubt we shall progress steadily and, I hope, fairly rapidly, in the future in the creation of these roads.

What has been said to-night rather reminds me of what was said yesterday: Each man for his own part of the country. It would seem that the members from the maritimes have not yet spoken on this subject, and I know they are anxious to do so. We have heard members from central Canada, from the prairies and some from British Columbia. As hon. members know, the greatest and most beautiful road in the world is now under construction, namely the road from Jasper to Banff, following the Columbia glacier. It presents the most magnificent scenery, so far as mountains are concerned, and would connect with the road system to which the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has referred. It also connects with the Jasper highway which goes directly to Edmonton.
Yesterday we heard a great deal of talk regarding the amount of money used for advertising in the United States and Great Britain to bring people to Canada to see the beauties of this country. From letters I have received from both the old country and the United 51952-1971
States, I am certain a large number of people are waiting the completion of this road which would go from Jasper to Lake Louise, following the ice-fields. I would ask the minister when he thinks the road would be completed, because I believe the work done on that road would prove most profitable in the near future through the number of people it would bring to that part of the country. Not only would it carry tourists, but it would also accommodate geologists and scientists. I know that at one time while I was in the mountains a thousand students came from the various universities of the United States to study geology, the ice age and so on. The road runs right along the great glaciers and, as I have said, it presents the most magnificent scenery in the great Rocky mountains system. I speak from knowledge, because I believe I have travelled from Utah north, through most of the mountains in the great Rocky mountains chain, and also along the coast range. If the minister could have the work completed quickly, it would prove most beneficial to that part of the country. Probably he is in a position to give the committee some information with respect to the road from Jasper, following the Columbia glacier to Lake Louise.

Hon. members in this section of the house do not wish to monopolize the attention of the committee, but I must remind hon. members that Alberta has a tremendous number of scenic beauties. We must not allow anybody to forget that, not because we wish to boast about it but because those beauties are a great national asset. I believe there are more parks in Alberta than in any other province. We are strategically located, particularly because we are near the Yellowstone national park. People come from all parts of the world to visit the Yellowstone park, from which with modern automobiles it is not a difficult or forbiddingly long trip to Glacier park. If there were a hard-surfaced road from the border towns of Coutts and Carway into Lethbridge and Cardston, it would invite many tourists who are now turned back as soon as they look across the Canadian border and see roads which yield dust. So important is this matter that I am taking it. upon myself to burden the committee a bit to-night by adding a third voice from Alberta urging that something be done soon. A good many people-and I do not include members of the house-do not realize that the tourist trade affects our trade balance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not our trade balance; it affects our balance of payments. That is a different matter.
Supply-National Parks
Yes; but there is an international balance between nations which is affected seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of payments.
Which is our chief anxiety.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One of them.

In the last analysis
it is the balance of payments which bothers us, and here is an excellent opportunity of overcoming what might become an adverse situation for Canada. Inasmuch as in this very year there are grave indications that we may have very trying times economically before we come together again, it might be worth while to readjust our plans to some extent this year so as to permit of the finishing of these roads from Coutts and Camay. It is not very far from Coutts to Lethbridge or from Camay to Cardston, and it would not be difficult to hard-surface the Kennedy creek cut-off road, which is another scenic attraction. I believe no expenditure in Canada would bring greater returns, unless it would be that particular portion mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), a portion with which I must admit I am not familiar.
I wish to add my voice to those which have been lifted in commendation of the efforts of the minister. So far as I have been able to find out, I believe, considering the money he has had at his disposal, he has administered his department very well. Nevertheless, I feel we will strengthen his hand with his fellow colleagues if we state that he needs even more money for the development of these roads and the encouragement of the tourist industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to say just a
few words which may be as much out of order as the remarks which cause me to make them. I gather that in the previous discussion the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard indicated that many desirable things could be done if it were not for-and I am not sure that this is the exact language-an inadequate Minister of Finance, and that he and other hon. members in the house would undertake to help the Minister of Mines and Resources in bringing about a reformation in that regard. In that connection I merely desire to point out that reformation is a very easy matter, if the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is speaking for any substantial number of members on the government side of the house, or, in fact, for any substantial number of members in 
the house. We still have responsible government in this country. The financial affairs of the country must be conducted in accordance with the principles of responsible government.
I do not believe that in those remarks the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard spoke for any considerable number of members supporting the government. Further, I do not believe that he spoke for the people of Canada. It will be very easy, Mr. Chairman, to discover either of those things. The hon. member has an opportunity of demonstrating the extent of the support which he could get for getting rid of the present Minister of Finance and the present financial methods of the country, and I hope he will attempt it, because then we shall have the house clearly on record as to whether the somewhat vague proposals of so-called financial reform, which I personally regard as financial reaction and not financial reform, should be applied in the proper constitutional manner by the government of Canada.
So far as I am concerned, I do not count. At this time I have a responsibility. It is not a responsibility which any man would seek in these times. It is a responsibility which I feel very keenly because of the debt I conceive I owe to Canada. In discharging it, I discharge it according to my conscientious belief as to what is best for Canada. But it is the function of this house to decide what is best for Canada; it is not my function or that of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. This house having decided what is best by way of financial policy, then the man who occupies the position which I occupy should be in accord with that policy. I am in accord, naturally, with the policy at present being followed.
Not in Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the Dominion of
Canada. Most certainly I am not in accord with the policy being followed in Alberta. But I am not responsible to the people of Alberta, as a province. I am responsible to them merely through their representatives in this house, in the same manner as I am responsible to the people of Canada through all the other representatives in the house. If at any time, which I would sincerely regret in what I believe to be the best interests of Canada, my hon. friends opposite who now occupy a few seats in the far comer should occupy the majority of seats in this house, they would expect to have a man sitting here who would carry into effect the policies in which the majority of that house believed. I am sure they would. I sincerely believe

Supply-National Parks
that I am putting into effect, and the government on my advice is following in matters of finance, a policy which is in accord with the wishes of the majority of members supporting the government in this house, and, indeed, far more than that. But I rose simply to say that there is an easy way to demonstrate whether or not that is the case.
In my few remarks this evening I regret very much that I have precipitated what appears to be a crisis in the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No crisis in the government.

I would never have thought that Garibaldi park would have figured so prominently in the politics of the dominion as that. I do want to take this opportunity of complimenting and congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the courageous and magnificent way in which he defends his conception of what his responsibilities are to this house, to his government, and to the people of the Dominion of Canada. But may I offer the suggestion, Mr. Chairman, that upon this question of public finance there may be good reasons why men even on the same side of politics may differ in the interpretation of the policy upon which this government was elected. It seems to me that I remember standing before my own electors, speaking throughout the province of British Columbia, and declaring that we were going to establish a reformed monetary system under which we were going to issue currency and credit through a national bank in terms of public need.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which we are doing.
And in terms of the social, economic and domestic needs of this nation.

Ninety
per cent of the Liberals thought that.
I want to say to my friends on the other side that I never knew of any suggestion on our part that we were only going to give national credit away for nothing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. gentleman take his seat for a moment? I think this discussion is entirely out of order. It is quite true that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard did bring in the monetary question. The Minister of Finance was not in his seat, and later he made a short reply, but this is not the time for this discussion. We are on the item, national parks bureau- national parks and historic sites services.
And the financing of them, as I understand, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. Order, please. I would ask all the members of the committee to confine their remarks to the item under discussion.
Mr. Chairman-

Wait a minute, please. I am not put out of the house just because I am out of order. Now that the Minister of Finance is in his place, may I offer to him for his consideration that if we could get the means of incorporating Garibaldi park within the administrative authority of the national Department of Mines and Resources, and if the same good policy of parks development and highway development to the parks were undertaken, it might prove a source of revenue that would more than justify the expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I was commenting on at all. I take no exception to that.
If we had this done, possibly we would find a source from which the revenues of the Department of Finance could be greatly enhanced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

I am satisfied that if the Minister of Finance were convinced of that, he would not hesitate to make the investment, because I think everyone will agree that even in national finance an investment that returns revenues, particularly when it is an investment that eliminates unemployment, and particularly also when it establishes a national asset of enduring value, is within the limits of the soundest and most orthodox finance. If I have any complaint to offer against the department, it is that they have not been awake to the opportunities of improving the revenues of the dominion, and I believe that Garibaldi park stands out as only one example of many that may be found in every province. May I say further to the Minister of Finance that such a program of development will meet with the unanimous approval of the whole people of the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You take in a lot of territory there.

I think what I have suggested is so sound that everybody would approve it. But when I rose to speak, I really did not have in mind the precipitation of any discussion on the administration of
Supply-National Parks

the Department of Finance per se, and may I apologize to the minister for having carelessly let go one or two shots that probably should have been reserved for the budget debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, you will allow me to accept the apology, and to say that I had no reference whatever to Garibaldi park or any other park but was referring simply to the suggestion made by my hon. friend that "we will make this antiquated Department of Finance" do something or another, and I was merely pointing out to the committee that there is a simple way for a majority of the members on this side of the house to determine the financial policy of the country. I was explaining how my hon. friend could obtain his wish. He will forgive me if I say he was taking in rather too much territory when he said: "we" will. "He" would, I have no doubt, but I doubt very much if he could associate with himself a sufficient number of members who think as he does to bring about the change which he indicated he so heartily desired.
Oh, do not take it too seriously.

I am not going to refer to the promises of the Liberal party before the election or get into a discussion of finance. I was interested in the observation of the minister that this year he expected to complete the road from Banff to Calgary, from Calgary to Waterton, and to connect up with the Glacier national park in the United States. Am I right?

My hon. friend is not quite right. I referred to the hard-surfaced road, all within Canadian territory, which was being constructed north of Kingsgate, and which, when completed, would lead into the parks sj'stem at Radium, out again to Calgary and on to Waterton lakes, then on to Glacier national park in the United States. That road will cover about six hundred miles, and I hope the program of work of hard-surfacing will be completed in a year.

Then I am right in
saying that as far as the expenditures this year are concerned, no money will be spent in connecting these parks with the boundary to the south; that is, outside the parks themselves?

No; I did not say that.
Part of the work will be carried on this year. It was carried on last year and the year before. We hope to finish it next year.

I notice in the supple-mentaries that there is considerable money 
to be spent. That road to which the minister is referring is mostly in British Columbia. I am talking about roads in Alberta connecting the boundary line with the parks. Will there be any work done on those highways?

That work was carried on
last year and the year previous under an arrangement with the Alberta government; that is the hard-surfacing from Calgary south to Waterton Park, and I expect that it will be continued this year. The national parks have the responsibility of doing the work from Waterton lakes to the international boundary, and we hope to get a start made on that this year.

It has been interesting to
listen to the remarks with reference to national parks in different parts of Canada and to hear the extravagant language used in describing each particular section-"most beautiful," "most magnificent," "most grand," an so on. But I wish to say, in the words of the poet Guest, that "you ain't been nowhere, you ain't seen nothin'," until you come down and see some of the beauties of the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And then go on to the Island.
A very good idea. Unfortunately, they are doing that now.
For a rest.

The minister has told us
that the proposed park in New Brunswick has been under consideration for some time. This, unfortunately, is very true; it has been "under consideration" now for at least three years, and it does not seem to be any nearer development now than it was three years ago. I am not blaming the federal minister for the situation, but I do blame those in authority in New Brunswick. I believe the interests of that province are being sacrificed by the provincial government, through the sectional jealousies and whims of various members of that government. When I make that statement I feel that, in the light of what has been happening for the past three years, I am doing no injustice to anyone.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard pointed out-a fact we all know-the great benefits which are being derived in Canada from our tourist trade. I believe he said that $300,000,000 is the revenue we receive from this source, and that possibly S180,000,-000 of that was net revenue to the people of the dominion. I want to point out to the committee that we in New Brunswick are not receiving a dollar of that revenue as

Supply-National Parks
far as parks is concerned. The importance of national parks cannot be overemphasized. There is at least one park in each province with the exception of New Brunswick and Quebec. I believe the minister earlier in the evening said there are twenty national parks in Canada, with an extent of some 12,500 square miles. A number of sites have been under consideration in New Brunswick. I do not think it should have been so difficult as it has been to decide upon one of those sites. When the matter of a national park for New Brunswick was considered, the neighbouring provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island were also considering national parks. Both of them have already established their parks, and development is well under way. I understand that Nova Scotia has one of the finest sites in Canada.
But I want to point out this: We have heard much about the construction of roads to give access to national parks. We in New Brunswick have been spending in the last few years millions of dollars in hard-surfacing roads, and at the present time we are doing it simply in order to send tourists to the national parks in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The situation is very unfair, and I hope that the minister, if he has any influence with the authorities in New Brunswick, will exert it and see that the in-justie which is being done to our province is remedied as soon as possible.	[DOT]
The importance of this matter in connection with the relief problem was emphasized this afternoon by the Minister of Labour when he stated, if I understood him correctly, that $3,000,000 would be expended on relief projects throughout Canada with relation to national parks. We in New Brunswick have not had direct relief in the last two years, though I venture to say that there has been as much destitution and as much need for relief in that province as in any other province of the dominion. It is a crying shame that the labouring men in New Brunswick are not in a position to-day to take advantage of some of this money which is being expended in different sections of Canada in developing parks. What is the situation at the present time with reference to the development of a national park in New Brunswick.

The problem in New
Brunswick is one of some difficulty. I understand the delay is due to the fact that, whatever site is selected, a considerable amount of private property will have to be re-possessed. My hon. friend is aware that the requirement is that the provincial government shall supply the area for development and convey the title
to that area to the federal government, whereupon the federal government will undertake the work of development.
Pardon me; is that not true of every national park which is established in Canada?
Quite.
Is the situation in New Brunswick any different from that in any other province?

If my hon. friend will allow me to continue for a moment, that was true- taking it as an illustration-in the Cape Breton island park in Nova Scotia, but in New Brunswick the matter of securing an area involves., as I understand it, re-possession by the government, through purchase or expropriation or whatever means they may take, of the private property at present within the area of the park which might be selected. As I understand it, that applies to any one of the areas which may be chosen. I appreciate the difficulties of the provincial government in that respect, because I understand the government of New Brunswick is a prudent government that does not wish unnecessarily to spend the taxpayers' money, and perhaps the worst criticism that might be directed against it is that it is proceeding with too much caution. However, I have no doubt that if that or any other criticism can be leveled against it for being rather dilatory in the matter, my hon. friend will take good care that the facts are presented to the people of New Brunswick as he has presented them here to-night, which of course is his privilege.
It is not facts of that kind the people of New Brunswick want. It is a park they want.

I quite understand that. After all, it is a matter of the province getting the area, and that is their business. I do not wish to criticize them, and certainly I have no wish to instruct them as to how they should proceed. What they should do is their business, not the business of the parks administration.
Is there anything further that the federal department needs to do?
No.
How many sites were inspected in New Brunswick, and what was the order in which they were selected by the federal department?

My recollection is that
four or five were examined, but at the moment
Supply-National Parks

I cannot recall the order of priority in which they were placed. My recollection is that that information was given in the discussion of the estimates a year ago.
No doubt the minister has the record there, and perhaps he will give it.

I am sorry I have not that information here; but when the supplementary estimates are up, there will be an opportunity again, to raise the question and I shall then have the information for the hon. member.

There was a vote of $25,000, I believe, either last year or the year before. How much of that has been expended, if any?
Mr. 'CRERAR: The vote was $25,000. It was put in for preliminary surveys that would be necessary before the active work of development would be undertaken. A similar vote is in the supplementary estimates for this year. It appeared in the special supplementary estimates a year ago. Once the area is selected, an accurate survey and an examination of the physical characteristics may be made, so that development can proceed in the best way in order to give the maximum result for the money expended. The amount in the supplementary estimates will cover the initial work in that respect, and that is the manner in which we have proceeded in all these matters. Once the initial survey is made and the data correlated, the parks officials are in a .position to recommend the type of development that should take place in order to get the maximum effect from the expenditure of the money.
I understand that the money provided in the supplementary estimates will be spent on an initial survey in New Brunswick. Is that correct?

We have included in our supplementary estimates the sum of $25,000. If the provincial government is in a position to turn over the area to us, then the money is available, once we know where we shall work, to make the initial surveys and to do the work I have mentioned.
Is it necessary for the provincial government to pass an act in the local legislature?
I understand that they have passed an act which will enable them to take appropriate action.
The hon. member may not be aware that the supplementary estimates were tabled this afternoon.
I said the special supplemen-taries.

I do not think there will be any further supplementaries, but he will observe that there is in the supplementary estimates an item for historic sites and monuments. I think I can say that when it comes to the allocation of that vote, the citadel at Halifax will not be overlooked.
What is the amount of money to be expended on each of the three national parks in Ontario?
Does the hon. member mean out of this vote?
Yes.
On Point Pelee park in lake Erie, $22,200; on the St. Lawrence islands, $3,500, and on the Georgian bay islands $4,000,

The Thirty Thousand islands district in Georgian bay is a very fine tourist centre, but those who live on those islands have much trouble in getting there on account of the difficulty of the channel. Tourists come there in great numbers from the United States as well as from Ontario, travelling by the boat from Midland. The difficulty is much greater at night. Would
it be possible to have the channel through those islands between Midland and Parry Sound, and up by Pointe au Baril, better buoyed? And if the channel were better lighted at night, many more people would be attracted to the islands.

The Department of Mines and Resources has nothing to do with the marking and lighting of channels. However, I shall be glad to bring my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the Minister of Transport, whose department has charge of that work.

I thank the minister for that assurance. I understand that one of the buoys marking the channel to Penetang harbour was taken away last year. I do not think it would cost very much to place more of those light buoys in that channel.

Are any negotiations being conducted with the province of British Columbia about a national park on Vancouver island? There is no need for me to descant on the glories of that place, after every other part of Canada has had its day. But some attention should be paid to the question of a national park on Vancouver island, especially now that we have learned that there are no national parks in British Columbia; that they are merely railway parks.

I do not agree with the view of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) in that connection. It may be that in the remote past, in the genesis of these parks in British Columbia, there was something to support the view he expressed, but I can assure the committee that now, at any rate, they are national parks. We realize they are when we have to devote money every year to their maintenance and administration. They are not in any sense railway parks.
As far as a park on Vancouver island is concerned, I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) a year or two ago advanced the claims of Vancouver island for recognition in that regard. Nothing further has been done. Of course the island itself is one vast park, and I do not know that an expenditure of federal money could very greatly improve its well known attractions.
Has work been commenced yet this spring on the gap in the Big Bend highway?

No. The vote for that work is in the supplementary estimates which were laid before the house this afternoon. I
Supply-National Parks

expect the work will start very shortly. The plans for it are complete, but we like to proceed in a manner that will not excite criticism on the part of our hon. friends opposite for proceeding in a non-orthodox fashion, and so we did not start this work until we had at any rate the estimates before the house. If my hon. friend feels like giving me an assurance that he would not criticize me for starting the work before the estimates were passed, we might consider getting it under way next week.
If I may interrupt, let me say that I would never criticize this government for moving too fast in anything.
My hon. friend, I am afraid, has not as much imagination as I thought.
One would need a lot of imagination to see any fast action in this matter.

If my hon. friend will
survey the record of the past two years of this department, I do not think he can seriously level that criticism against it. However, speaking more seriously, we do hope to get the work there started very shortly.

I was in Revelstoke during the Easter recess, and people there told me that conditions were such that the work could be started, but nothing had been done, and apparently it takes some time to get the work camps established. Is it the intention of the government to complete the gap this year? I believe there are only about thirty-three miles to finish.

I am afraid it cannot be
completed this year. There is a good deal of very heavy construction, and it is through difficult country, as my hon. friend knows. If you have to push your work and machines and equipment very far in advance of the road as completed, it adds greatly to the expense. We shall not be able to complete it this year, but certainly it is the intention to have it completed next year. I am a little disappointed that we have not made more rapid progress; but last September I went right to the end of that road, where they were pulling out stumps, cutting down great, heavy trees and clearing rock cuts from Revelstoke north. I saw for myself the extremely difficult nature of the country through which they are building, and taking all the facts into consideration I think the progress with that road has been very good.

I realize that is an extremely difficult piece of construction, but I would suggest that the minister give serious con-
sideration to finishing the gap this year. I am quite sure that once the gap is completed, a great deal of the difficulty mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard will be done away with, because then the people of the coast, not only from British Columbia but also from the Pacific states, will be able to drive up to the national parks. Then we shall realize that the parks in the Rockies are really British Columbia parks.

Well, I should like very
much to see that completed this year, but I would not be quite frank with my hon. friend if I gave him any impression that this would be the case. Quite frankly, I do not think it can be, but as I said a moment ago I certainly hope it will be completed next year.
How is the work progressing on the road between Banff and Jasper national parks, and when will it be completed.

Precisely the same conditions are met with there that we find on the so-called Big Bend road; that is, the Jasper-Banff road has been built from both ends. Work has proceeded from the Jasper end and from the Banff end ever since the road was started, and there is still a considerable gap remaining; I believe some thirty miles remain to be completed. That, also, is very heavy construction. I may tell my hon. friend that I was also over both ends of that road last September. I like to get out and see the work that is going on and the nature of the difficulties that have to be overcome. The remaining portion of that road is very heavy construction, a great deal of it being rock work and the clearing of timber. In that class of construction, unless you are prepared to throw money around rather freely, it is not possible to make rapid progress, but I think I can say to the committee that, it is the intention to have that road also completed next year.

May I ask what
the amount of $22,200 for Pelee island is expended for, and also the $4,000 for the Georgian bay islands and the $3,500 for the St. Lawrence islands?

It is for general administrative work. The administrative costs in the islands, both in the St. Lawrence and in Georgian bay, are not very heavy, and consequently the vote is small. At Point Pelee, as my hon. friend is probably aware, there is heavy tourist traffic during the summer months, and the cost of administrative work is heavier. The amount is divided thus:

Supply-National Parks
Management and clerical work, $8,900; public services, $11,200; and those comprise water, roads and bridges, health, sanitation, camp grounds, gateways and information bureaux. The other items are: Stores and equipment, $2,000, and a small item for garage and repair shop, warehouses, stores and mechanical equipment. This amount has been increased in the supplementary estimates which were tabled this afternoon.
Is this expenditure on the Thirty Thousand islands of Georgian bay in connection with game wardens or something like that?

I can give my hon. friend the particulars:	Administration, $3,190; office
expense, $400; garages and repair shops, $200; warehouses and stores, $210.

I should like to say a further word in regard to the Georgian bay lights. Very often in that country one cannot get down in the daytime, but the wind goes down at night and you can get through. I think lives would be saved if there were lights so that people could travel at night rather than during the daytime. I want again to urge the importance of better lighting for the channel through the Thirty Thousand islands and also around by Point au Baril.
I shall see that my hon. friend's suggestion is placed before the Department of Transport, which has to do with these matters.
I should like to ask one more question about the Big Bend road. Is British Columbia contributing any portion of the cost on the west side?
No.
It is entirely borne by the dominion government?
That expense is borne by the federal government.

That agreement fell
through?

My recollection is that the arrangement was made by the late government to build the west leg. The original arrangement was made when my right hon. leader was Prime Minister previously, to build the east leg, and the provincial government is bearing no part of the cost of construction. Under the agreement, when the road is constructed it will be taken over by the provincial government, and of course thereafter the cost of maintenance will be their responsibility.
From the edge of the park?

No; from Golden to
Revelstoke.
Through the national park?

No; we did not undertake the obligation to build the portion of the road from the west gate of the park to Golden. The original arrangement covered from Donald to the crossing of the Canoe river. Later, that was extended to cover the portion between Golden and Donald. Then, during the administration of the present right hon. leader of the opposition the arrangement with British Columbia was extended to cover the portion of the road from the crossing at Canoe river down to Revelstoke, and the expense of that construction is being wholly borne by the federal government.

Since some of the discussion on this item has developed in connection with points of interest having particular reference to historical spots, I want to bring to the attention of the minister a place in western Nova Scotia where it is claimed the first white man landed in North America. There are records in the old country describing the voyage and the shore where the landing was made, and that description exactly fits this location in western Nova Scotia. We also have a runic stone, where they are supposed to have landed, bearing an inscription which they marked at the time. According to the records, that landing is presumed to have been in the year 1006, the first landing of the Norsemen in North America, actually the first white men to come here from Europe. I have no doubt that the development of a place of that kind would prove a spot of historical interest, and would help develop the tourist trade.

Item agreed to.
Administration of Migratory Birds Convention Act, $51,000.

This item has to do with the administration of the migratory birds convention between Canada and the United States. In the present year there is a slight increase in the vote. I assume at least part of that is due to the restoration of the salary cuts and to the ordinary statutory increases in salaries. I believe there was the appointment of one additional stenographer. That is an expense which under the Migratory Birds Convention Act we are obligated to carry out.
Supply-Migratory Birds

I have no fault to find with the vote, but the report has got about in British Columbia that there is a chance of the administration of this act being turned over to the provinces. I have a protest from an angling and game association in Vancouver against the administration being turned over to the provinces. I hope there is no question of that being done.

The hon. member's remarks are the first I have heard to that effect. I can assure him there is no intention of doing anything of the kind. As a matter of fact, 1 do not think we could turn over to a province the administration of an international obligation with the United States.

It has been called to my attention that last year two or three hunters got into trouble through lack of knowledge of the law. We realize, of course, that is no excuse. The laws with respect to duck shooting were published by the province of Ontario. There are also certain variations or extensions in the law which are made under the Migratory Birds Convention Act. I understand the regulations are posted up by the federal government, but it is very difficult for a hunter to look on the telegraph posts to find out what those regulations may be. Could some arrangement not be made between the provincial and federal governments for the combining of the provincial and federal laws?
I should also like to learn how the enforcement of the act is carried out. Do the provinces do it; is it a combination between the provinces and the dominion, or is it done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

In most provinces the regulations agreed upon by the federal and provincial authorities are enforced by the province. There are certain cases where enforcement is carried out by the mounted police. We aim to get cooperation with the provinces, and have been very successful in that regard. The regulations framed from year to year govern particularly the hunting of wild fowl. We have not run into any difficulty in connection with the administration of the act. I think almost everyone from one end of Canada to the other is seized with the importance of preserving the migratory birds. I might point out further that opinion in the United States has crystallized into a more strict enforcement of regulations than obtained several years ago. I believe they are now doing their full share.

Is there any danger from the shooting of ducks and other types

of game which takes place in James bay? In the minds of some people there seems to be a certain amount of apprehension with respect to the preservation of ducks and other types of wild fowl. They feel that the hunting in the feeding grounds in James bay will have a serious effect on the wild fowl population.

That matter has been discussed with the Ontario authorities; but, for the greater part, I believe the migratory birds go farther north for nesting and rearing their young. I am informed that the James bay situation, to which the hon. member has just referred, is being discussed between the Ontario government and the federal department.
Were any new bird sanctuaries established during the past year?

I am advised there were a few established, but I cannot give the hon. member exact information in that regard. I should be glad to supply it when the supple-mentaries are under consideration. If the hon. member will raise the question at that time, I shall be pleased to answer it.

I believe that during the last few years there has been some conflict in connection with the game regulations in British Columbia. I have received representations similar to those indicated by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I endorse the statement that the administration of the act should be carried on by the federal government. I should like to know what the conflict was; I know there was some conflict in connection with the game regulations.

The only question of conflict which arose was that some of the hunters in British Columbia were not quite satisfied with the periods of open and closed seasons which were established. It is only very rarely that all of the regulations in any province are accepted without at least some criticism. I must add, however, that the general good sense of the public supports the regulations as they are framed from year to year.

Item agreed to.
Grant to John Thomas (Jack) Miner, $4,000.
This is the usual grant.
I suppose there will be supplementary estimates under which we shall be able to discuss almost anything pertaining to the department.

Yes.

I would be very glad to accede to the suggestion of the hon. member, and I would do so particularly because I know of the interest of the right hon. the leader of the opposition in the Banff national park and in western parks generally.
